name: Efton Chism III
summary: Efton (EFF-tun) Chism (Chiz-um) III was born in Kirkland, Wash., with his parents (Efton and Kristy) and started playing football in eighth grade. He was an all-league player in baseball, basketball and football at Monroe High. A three-star recruit, Chism had an FBS offer from Air Force but grew up watching Eastern Washington games, and that program "felt like home." He put together a record-breaking college career, including a catch in 53 straight games to break Cooper Kupp's previous FCS mark. THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 137 Chism is a slick route runner with craftsman hands and commendable toughness working into the teeth of the defense. Though he has better play strength than most slots, he is a smaller target and will face a substantial jump in the talent level against NFL defensive backs. He also returned punts in college but averaged just 4.6 yards per attempt. Overall, Chism is the quintessential quicker-than-fast slot receiver, with lagging deep speed but dazzling feet in and out of breaks to give his quarterback quick windows.

name: Will Sheppard
summary: Will Sheppard, one of three children, was born in Ruston, La., with his parents (Willie Sheppard and Rebekah Boyd), both college athletes at Louisiana Tech. At Mandeville High, Sheppard was a three-sport star (62 receptions for 1,276 yards and 24 touchdowns as a senior). A three-star recruit, he committed to Vanderbilt and produced for three straight years on a struggling offense. He transferred to Colorado for his senior year and was Shedeur Sanders' third-leading receiver in 2024. While seeing heavy doses of slants and back-shoulder throws, Sheppard uses his frame well to shield defenders and catch the football away from his body. That ability shows in the red zone — 17 of his 23 touchdown grabs the past three years came inside the opponent's 20.. Though drops were an issue for him in 2023, his hands were sticky on the 2024 tape and he caught the ball cleanly over/around defenders. Overall, Sheppard doesn't have dynamic speed, and detaching from NFL athleticism won't be easy for him, but he is a seasoned route runner with the hand-eye coordination to be a potential possession target.

name: Jackson Meeks
summary: Jackson Meeks, the nephew of NFL defensive end Za'Darius Smith, grew up with his mother (Genniefer) in Phenix City, Ala. He posted moderate receiving production at Central High but went overlooked by instate powers Alabama and Auburn. A three-star recruit, he was hoping to play in the SEC and committed to Georgia within a week of being offered his senior season. After three years (and two national championships) as a backup, Meeks entered the transfer portal and found a friendly face in former Georgia assistant Fran Brown, who took over as the Syracuse head coach in 2024. With fellow transfer Kyle McCord at quarterback, Meeks eclipsed 1,000 yards receiving in THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 138 2024. He isn't a polished separator in his routes, but he is physical to the football to pluck and ﬁnish (No. 2 in the FBS in 2024 with 21 contested catches). His body strength shows mid-route, over the middle and after the catch (Brown: "He's a dog."). Overall, Meeks isn't a burner, which will limit his role at the next level, but he plays with the competitive juices, decisive movements and ball skills to be a chain-moving option.

name: Roc Taylor
summary: Rokafewlloa "Roc" Taylor, the youngest of four, grew up in Oxford, Ala., with his mother (Christina). He started playing football at age 4 and was an all-state receiver as a junior at Oxford High (1,291 receiving yards). A three-star recruit, Taylor was committed to Tennessee for more than 18 months, but the school rescinded his offer days before signing day after a coaching change. Taylor landed at Memphis instead and combined for 2,033 receiving yards over his junior and senior seasons. Taylor has the look of an NFL receiver with his long, muscled-up frame — and the way he extends outside that frame to snatch the football. His hand-eye coordination shows in crowded environments, although it also shines a light on his struggles to set up defenders and easily separate at the tops of routes. Overall, Taylor will struggle to escape press and tight coverage over the ﬁrst two levels, but his competitiveness and ability to adjust to the football will be his tickets to success at the next level, especially in the red zone.

name: Traeshon Holden
summary: Traeshon Holden, originally from Florida, played for Biff Poggi at St. Frances Academy in Baltimore. He transferred to Narbonne High in Los Angeles for his senior year and caught 31 passes for 512 yards and seven touchdowns. A four-star recruit, he committed to Alabama, where THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 139 he was roommates with Bryce Young and ﬁlled in when Jaylen Waddle was injured in 2020. After three years in Tuscaloosa, he transferred to Oregon before the 2023 season. Despite a rocky start there, he set career bests as a senior. Holden gives his quarterback a large target and is at his best on digs and crossers, attacking the teeth of the defense. He stays coordinated in his releases and route entrance but lacks the speed or suddenness to easily separate, especially on the ﬁrst and second levels. Overall, Holden will have a tough time detaching from NFL corners, but he produces when he plays to his play strength and physicality. The interview vetting process will be pivotal for him.

name: Josh Kelly
summary: Joshua "Josh" Kelly, who has an older brother (Chris), grew up in California with his parents (Chris and De'Andra). He moved to wide receiver in high school at Bullard High before transferring to San Joaquin Memorial for his senior year, posting 1,127 receiving yards in 2018. A three-star recruit, he stayed close to home and played at Fresno State, catching passes from Jake Haener. After an injury-riddled 2022 season, Kelly transferred to Washington State in 2023, then to Texas Tech for his ﬁnal season — he posted career-best numbers out of the slot in 2024. Kelly isn't the most detailed or explosive route runner, but his stem breaks are sharp because of his quick, urgent feet. Despite a relatively lean frame, he owns large, conﬁdent hands and works well with bodies around him to ﬁnish in traffic. Overall, Kelly ﬂashes elusiveness before and after the catch, but his lack of desired speed (on tape and the stopwatch) is a high hurdle that will be tough to clear versus NFL coverage.

name: Dymere Miller
summary: Dymere (die-meer) Miller grew up outside of Philadelphia, with his mother (Chaquita). After a car accident sidelined him for a stretch at Coatesville High, he attended Salisbury for a post-graduate year in 2019 and put himself on the radar of several FCS schools. He signed with Monmouth and set single-season school records for catches and receiving yards. For his ﬁnal season, he jumped into the portal and committed to Rutgers over Memphis, Pitt and Texas Tech. He led Rutgers in receiving in 2024. Miller is both quick and fast to pace his routes, cross up corners and create passing windows for the quarterback, which is necessary since he is a smaller target. Despite his movement skills, he wasn't very elusive on his 2024 tape and got himself in trouble by taking his eyes off the ball too quickly, leading to drops. Overall, Miller needs to be more reliable putting catches away, but the athletic talent is NFL-worthy in the slot and gives him upside on special teams coverages.

name: Mac Dalena
summary: Mac Dalena, the third of four kids, was raised in Fresno, Calif., by his parents (Brian and Lisa). His older brother (Frank) also played wide receiver at Fresno State (2015-19). Mac Dalena caught 69 passes for 1,212 yards and 19 touchdowns as a senior captain at San Joaquin Memorial High (also had seven interceptions and was the 2018 baseball player of the year). A three-star recruit, Dalena went widely overlooked, but not by his hometown Fresno State, which was his ﬁrst offer. After playing mostly on special teams for three years, he became a full-time starter in 2023 and had a career year in 2024. Dalena has the size of a slot but lined up mostly outside (89.2 percent of his snaps were wide), where he used his speed to create quick separation underneath or win vertically (one of just seven FBS receivers with at least ﬁve catches of 50 yards or more in 2024). He has reliable hands and can use his body, when necessary, to ﬁnish (only four drops on 178 career targets) His catch radius is small, though, and off-target throws often stay that way. Overall, Dalena can ﬁght for a slot role in the NFL, but his special teams experience (17 tackles, one blocked punt on 605 special teams snaps) will separate him.

name: Tyler Warren
strengths: ● Well-built athlete with a prototypical frame for tight end duties ● Builds acceleration quickly to enter his route and attack coverage ● Fluid movement skills for a big man, with the foot quickness to get in and out of breaks ● Above-average hand-eye coordination to securely snatch the football in stride ● Had more one-handed grabs than drops on his 2024 ﬁlm ● Maintains focus with congested catch points or impending contact ● Comfortable leaving his feet and has the body ﬂexibility to high-point or adjust to off-target throws ● Has some wiggle after the catch (56.2 percent of receiving yards in 2024 came post-catch) ● Lowers pads to ﬁnish through contact — it often required gang tackles to get him down ● Effective wildcat option; averaged 8.4 yards per carry in 2024 (26 carries for 218 yards and four touchdowns) ● Lefty passer; completed three of his six passes for 35 yards in 2024, including a 17-yard touchdown ● Takes pride in blocking responsibilities (models his game after George Kittle) ● Delivers pop on wham blocks and looks to drive his legs in the run game ● Laid-back, unassuming and avoids the spotlight (not on social media), but he's competitive on the football ﬁeld (nickname in the Penn State tight end room was "Psycho T"). ● Fourth tight end in FBS history to reach 104 catches in a single season ● Routinely plays through minor injuries and doesn't miss games
weaknesses: ● Average arm length and needs to be quicker with his hands into blocks ● Guilty of head ducking and sacriﬁcing his balance once engaged with defenders ● Only 5.9 percent of targets the past two seasons came 20 yards or more down the ﬁeld (64.1 percent came within 9 yards of the line) ● Occasionally will hurry through routes, rounding breaks and giving clues to defenders ● Attempts to match physical coverage, which causes him to be late turning his head for the football
summary: A two-year starter at Penn State, Warren was used across the formation in offensive coordinator Andy Kotelnicki's scheme and saw manufactured touches, splitting his snaps between inline, slot, wide and in the backﬁeld (also took 40 wildcat snaps in short-yardage or goal-line situations in 2024). A high school quarterback, he joined a Penn State tight end room that included four future NFL Draft picks (Pat Freiermuth, Brenton Strange, Zack Kuntz and Theo Johnson) and became the best college player of the group. He rewrote the tight end record books at Penn State, including the single-game, single-season and career receiving records (ﬁnished seventh in 2024 Heisman Trophy voting, highest for a tight end since 1977). A high-efficiency pass catcher, Warren moves with light feet, ﬂuid body movements and natural balance, all of which helps him instantly transition from receiver to runner and become a threat with the ball in his hands. He showed improved trust in his hands as a senior and now calmly adjusts to ﬁnish catches regardless of the traffic around him (three drops on 135 targets in 2024). Though he's aggressive as a blocker, he will fall off run blocks and needs improved positioning/footwork through contact. Overall, Warren still has developing to do as a route runner and blocker, but he is an agile-footed big man who naturally tracks the football with dependable hands and a hunger to create after the catch. He projects as a rookie NFL starter with traditional qualities, as well as the schematic versatility to be a multi-tool weapon for a play caller.

name: Colston Loveland
strengths: ● Fluid, fast athlete who is graceful down the seam ● Explosive in releases to quickly enter routes and give quarterback a target ● Can win on slants or posts one-on-one against cornerbacks ● Makes deft moves to set up defenders, snap breaks and create versus man coverage ● Efficient on slam-ﬂat plays to engage/sell edge defenders before releasing into space ● Sticky hands — catching radius and leaping ability were tested often by erratic quarterback play ● Plays with toughness over the middle and bounces back after hits ● Can leapfrog defenders or use stiff arm to battle for extra yards ● Shows good ﬁght as blocker in run game ● Penalized just once over past two seasons (illegal formation that wasn't his fault) ● His coaches praise how much he puts into craft (Michigan coach Sherrone Moore: "The guy just works, he works, he works. Reminds me of Blake Corum.") ● Set Michigan single-season record for catches by a tight end (despite missing chunks of time) THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 152
weaknesses: ● Lean body type, lacking ideal mass for NFL inline work ● Mediocre play strength limits effectiveness as sustain blocker ● Needs to focus on keeping low base and tighter hands as run blocker ● Can be displaced from spot by middling contact in pass protection ● Low batting average in contested situations (caught only two of 10 contested targets in 2024) ● Struggles to avoid tacklers after the catch without a runway ● Just 12.5 percent of 2024 catches resulted in 20 yards or more ● Missed three games (and parts of several other games) because of right shoulder injury (Sept. 2024); AC joint surgery in Jan. 2025, which sidelined him for the draft process (on track to be cleared for training camp); missed Ohio State game because of concussion (Nov. 2024)
summary: A three-year starter at Michigan, Loveland was a versatile tight end in head coach Sherrone Moore's pro-style scheme, lining up primarily in the slot (47.6 percent of the time) and inline/wing (32.5 percent) as a junior. From the moment he arrived in Ann Arbor, he was one of the most talented players on the roster and made an immediate impact his ﬁrst two years, including as the Wolverines' leading receiver in the 2023 national championship game. His ﬁnal season was marred by injury and below-average quarterback play, but he still led the team in receiving in nine of the 10 games he played and set Michigan records for the tight end position. With his speed and ball skills, Loveland can line up anywhere on the ﬁeld and win as a quarterback-friendly, multilevel receiving threat. He isn't a liability as a one-pop, get-in-the-way blocker but will struggle to sustain or control NFL edge defenders. Overall, Loveland doesn't have the skill set for full-time inline responsibilities, but his dynamic movements, natural hands and football awareness should make him one of the primary targets in an NFL offense. His tools and upside are reminiscent of Zach Ertz.

name: Mason Taylor
strengths: ● Athletic big man who is still growing into his frame ● Dependable hands and naturally adjusts to throws away from his body ● Focus doesn't ﬂinch in traffic ● Cleanly frames and catches in stride for quick transitions to running after catch ● Secures through contact to withstand crushing hits ● Runs smooth routes and quickly gets his head turned to make himself available ● Strong positional blocker to shield and steer ● Understands angles and is effective as a stalk blocker, especially on the perimeter ● Started right away in the SEC and caught a pass in 37 of 38 career games ● Ranks ﬁrst (55), third (38) and fourth (36) in single-season catches by an LSU tight end
weaknesses: ● Shaky base and anchor in pass protection ● Too easily bullied or tossed aside by defensive ends, especially when his hands land wide ● Found end zone only once every 21.5 catches ● Follows blocks well as a ball carrier but didn't create much yards after catch in 2024 ● Didn't create many explosive plays (six of 55 catches in 2024 went for 20 yards or more) ● False starts on back-to-back snaps against UCLA (and another against Arkansas) ● Never recorded a 100-yard receiving game in college ● Missed one game as sophomore and parts of others because of ankle sprain (Sept. 2023) ● Didn't play on special teams in college
summary: A three-year starter at LSU, Taylor was a versatile tight end in offensive coordinator Joe Sloan's pass-happy offense (55.7 percent of snaps inline, 37.0 percent in the slot in 2024). Known more for being the son of a Pro Football Hall of Famer when he enrolled, Taylor made a name for himself by becoming the most productive tight end in LSU history — he set records for career catches (129) and receiving yards (1,308). Despite those achievements, his single-game high in receiving yards was just 63 (vs. Georgia in 2022). Taylor is a loose mover, which shows in his route running and at the catch point, and he has the hand-eye coordination to make natural adjustments and ﬁnish in traffic. In the run game, he is more of a wall-off blocker than a violent people-mover, but his toughness and athleticism at the point of attack help him execute his assignments, especially out in space as a move blocker. Overall, Taylor was Mr. Reliable in the LSU offense — and can be the same for an NFL team, because of his his good-sized athleticism, reliable ball skills and competitive blocking. He projects as a solid NFL starter who doesn't have to leave the ﬁeld and has some similarities to Hunter Henry.

name: Elijah Arroyo
strengths: ● Fluid, loose athlete for the position with above-average speed ● Strides are light and long, which allows him to eat up ground quickly and be a factor on seams, posts and fades ● 34.3 percent of his catches in 2024 went for 20 yards or more (for context, Brock Bowers ﬁnished his ﬁnal season at Georgia at 23.2 percent) ● Impressive pacing on one- and two-cut routes, where he can shake and separate ● Strong focus and hands (only one career drop), no matter the action required ● Secures ball well in stride to be a catch-and-go weapon (led FBS tight ends in 2024 with 9.1 yards after catch/reception) ● Competes as a blocker, both when driving inline or out in space ● Was 220 pounds when he enrolled in college and found good balance of adding weight without sacriﬁcing speed ● Served as a team captain for four games in 2024 (Mario Cristobal: "That guy's the ultimate team player. He's been through a lot, and he's seen ups and downs. He's just really hungry for team success.")
weaknesses: ● Doesn't have the most expansive college resume (46 catches over four seasons) ● Saw a lot of free releases in college ● Often revealed his intentions too early and has room to grow as a route runner ● Hardly any examples on tape of him making grabs in traffic ● Positions himself to stalemate defenders as a blocker, but he's not a power player ● Needs more consistent technique as an on-the-move blocker on split zones ● Missed most of the 2022 and 2023 seasons after suffering torn ACL in his left knee (September 2022)
summary: A one-year starter at Miami (Fla.), Arroyo was an F tight end in offensive coordinator Shannon Dawson's RPO-based version of the Air Raid, lining up mostly in the slot (51.6 percent of snaps) and occasionally inline (39.4 percent). He had just 16 combined targets over his ﬁrst three seasons with the Hurricanes as he battled a knee injury, but then delivered a breakout 2024, leading the FBS in yards per catch among tight ends (16.9). An awesome athlete at 250 pounds, Arroyo gets in and out of his breaks with efficiency and speed to consistently create separation, which makes him a threat to score any time he touches the ball (71.4 percent of his catches in 2024 resulted in a ﬁrst down or touchdown). He will need to prove himself through contact in the passing game at the next level, where he won't be given as much space to operate. Overall, Arroyo needs further development as a route runner and blocker to reach his ceiling, but he can bring an immediate vertical element to an offense with his speed, ﬂuidity and focused ball skills. He is easy to project as an NFL starter and a weapon for which defenses must account.

name: Terrance Ferguson
strengths: ● Athletic pass catcher to snatch and immediately get upﬁeld ● Natural hand-eye coordination to scoop or reach back and bring in throws ● Knows where the sticks are and consistently gets hidden yards (72.1 percent of his catches in 2024 resulted in a ﬁrst down or touchdown) ● Runs physical routes and doesn't allow safeties to muscle him off his path ● Subtle foot quickness in and out of breaks — able to sink and break opposite to create a passing window ● Functional strength as a base blocker, inline and out in space ● Shows blocking range out of the slot on swing screens ● Willing run blocker who will get his face dirty and showcase toughness at the point of attack
weaknesses: ● Too much of one-speed athlete ● Needs better salesmanship and pacing to hide route intentions ● Physical ﬁnisher as a ball carrier but needs to use athleticism more to sidestep tacklers ● Below average in contested situations senior season ● Engages well as blocker but will struggle to control defenders ● Put some weak, chicken-wing chips on tape ● Much better home-game performer (80 percent of catches in 2024 and 13 of 16 career touchdown grabs came at Oregon's Autzen Stadium) ● Missed two games as senior because of appendectomy (Oct. 2024); missed second half of UCLA game with head injury (Sept. 2024) THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 156
summary: A four-year starter at Oregon, Ferguson was a versatile tight end in offensive coordinator Will Stein's spread scheme, lining up for 42.0 percent of his 2024 snaps in the slot and 40.5 percent inline/wing (often used as a blocker for a two count before releasing as a target). Although his senior season didn't quite reach the heights scouts were hoping for, he was a dependable target and his role continued to expand. A high school hooper, Ferguson displays athleticism both as a route runner and after the catch, along with steady ball skills (25.6 percent of his catches in 2024 resulted in 20 yards or more). He needs technical work (tighter hands and feet) as a blocker but ﬁnds ways to stalemate defenders. Overall, there isn't much about his game that screams "exceptional," but Ferguson is solid across the board and should continue to ascend as he adds consistency to his blocking and patterns. He has the foundational traits to carve out an NFL career similar to that of Jake Ferguson (no relation).

name: Harold Fannin Jr.
strengths: ● Straight-line explosiveness; plays with athletic urgency into routes ● Uses speed to challenge defenses, vertically and horizontally ● Run after catch was a key ingredient to his college success ● Body quickness to manipulate space, which helps him get free or force missed tackles ● Physical stiff arm with run balance to carry tacklers for extra yards ● Secure hands catcher and comfortable playing through contact ● Catches just about everything in catch radius, because of his adjustment skills ● Nice range as a puller on sweeps/pitches or as a lead blocker on split zone or iso THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 157 ● Set almost every Bowling Green receiving record for a tight end ● Dominated against MAC competition; also played at a high level vs. Penn State (11 catches, 137 yards, one TD) and Texas A&M (eight catches, 145 yards, one TD) in 2024 ● Moved all around in Bowling Green's scheme (third-highest rate for lining up wide among all FBS tight ends in 2024)
weaknesses: ● Lacks desired size for inline work ● Duck-footed — often runs with feet often pointed outwards, which dulls route breaks ● Route movements appear stiff and rigid, with excess limb waste ● Physical defenders can too easily grind his momentum down at top of the route ● Doesn't have stout frame or body strength to consistently seal NFL ends ● Inconsistent breaking down as a blocker in space
summary: A two-year starter at Bowling Green, Fannin played the "A" tight end position in head coach Scot Loeffler's pro-style spread offense, splitting his snaps between inline/wing (38.3 percent), slot (31.7 percent) and out wide (26.2 percent). In an offense designed to weaponize its tight end, Fannin transitioned from high school safety and had arguably the greatest tight end season in FBS history in 2024, setting single-season records for catches (117) and receiving yards (1,555). He became the ﬁrst consensus All-American in Bowling Green history (and just the school's second in any sport). With his strong hands and urgent athleticism, Fannin is at his best as a pass catcher and shows a unique feel for creating as a ball carrier. He is still very young — and it shows, especially in his blocking and route running. Overall, Fannin is somewhat of an unconventional prospect. He is awkwardly athletic with stiff, restricting movements, but he plays with straight-line explosiveness, outstanding tracking skills and threatening run-after-catch ability. He ﬁts best as a hybrid H or F tight end and offers three-down potential.

name: Gunnar Helm
strengths: ● Balanced big man with a workable frame and length ● Quick out of his stance and very efficient with releases, regardless of where he lines up ● Creates leverage out of breaks ● Has a knack for working himself open in the scramble drill ● Natural catcher of the football and very conﬁdent at the catch point (2.5 percent career drop rate) ● Outstanding vision to be a threat after the catch (420 yards after catch in 2024, third most among FBS tight ends) ● Has natural coordination to elude, hurdle or slip tackle attempts ● Physical, try-hard blocker who loses slowly in pass protection ● Comfortable getting to the second level and walling off linebackers ● Not the most vocal but prototypical "lead by example" guy — doesn't have any knucklehead in him ● Smart and competitive (tight end is the second-hardest position to grasp in Sarkisian's offense, behind quarterback)
weaknesses: ● Below-average speed for the position, especially for a player with his size proﬁle ● Doesn't have pop or power to consistently overwhelm and move defenders in run game ● Head-ducker into contact as a move blocker, often losing sight of his target ● Vastly improved hand placement on 2024 tape, but there is still room to get better (ﬂagged for holding three times in 2024) ● Sack allowed against Georgia in the SEC Championship Game showed some of his issues in pass pro ● Occasionally rounds his stem — still ﬁne-tuning his route-tree footwork ● Only one season of high-level receiving production
summary: A two-year starter at Texas, Helm was a versatile tight end in head coach Steve Sarkisian's RPO pro-style spread offense and was used across the formation with heavy motions (68.3 percent of snaps inline, 22.0 percent slot, 9.7 percent wide). With just 22 combined targets over his ﬁrst three seasons in Austin, he went overlooked in the shadow of Ja'Tavion Sanders, but the coaches say he maxed out his work each day to steadily improve and be ready for his moment. He became "the guy" as a senior and didn't disappoint, emerging as the offense's most consistent aspect and leading the team in receptions. More balanced than explosive as an athlete, Helm does a great job ﬁnding space in coverage and contorting his body to adjust and ﬁnish the catch. With his knack for giving defenders the slip, he is one of the best tight ends in this draft class after the catch. Overall, Helm will need time to adjust to NFL physicality as a blocker, but he has the toughness and pass-catching talent to potentially become a three-down player. His tape shows a possible mismatch weapon, but his lackluster combine performance will give NFL teams pause.

name: Oronde Gadsden II
strengths: ● Tall, rangy athlete who has worked hard to add bulk ● Terriﬁc hand strength to ﬁnish catches through contact ● Coordinated body control to locate and adjust to throws mid-route ● Ranked second in 2024 among FBS tight ends with 17 contested catches ● Foot quickness helps him enter routes and create separation out of breaks ● Displays overall movement skills of former wide receiver ● Responsible for 16 catches of 20 yards or more in 2024 (fourth most among FBS tight ends) ● Willing positional blocker — can get in the way and seal off ● At best as backside run blocker or on the move ● Most productive tight end in Syracuse history
weaknesses: ● Doesn't have desired frame or body mass for the position ● Relies more on athleticism than pacing or technique in route stems ● Marginal after-the-catch threat with ball in his hands ● Not the type of ball carrier who will frequently run through tackles ● Needs to continue developing football-playing strength to sustain (never lined up inline until 2024) ● Works to keep hands tight and chop feet but not a people mover in run game ● Lisfranc injury in right foot (Sept. 2023), which required season-ending surgery
summary: A two-year starter at Syracuse, Gadsden was a joker tight end in offensive coordinator Jeff Nixon's pro-spread system (58.3 percent of his snaps aligned in the slot, 32.6 percent inline, 8.7 percent wide in 2024). A wide receiver when he enrolled, Gadsden transitioned to a hybrid tight end role as a sophomore and had the two most productive seasons (2022, 2024) for a tight end in school history (with a season-ending injury in between, in 2023). Like his father, who played in the NFL for several seasons, Gadsden is the type of target who doesn't require his quarterback to be perfect because of the way he uses his frame, focus and long arms to pull in throws. Though he has functional athleticism as a route runner, his setup and pacing are still in the developmental phase. I was expecting more after the catch, too (just 27.5 percent of his yards in 2024 came with the ball in his hands, one of the lowest rates in the FBS). As a blocker, he gives quality effort and can get in the way, but he won't consistently move defenders at the point of attack in the run game. Overall, Gadsden is an athletic pass catcher with the adjustment skills and catch radius to be a possession target in an NFL offense, although his average frame and marginal ability to sustain blocks create questions about his role. He projects best as an F tight end who can be ﬂexed across the formation and should continue to get better.

name: Mitchell Evans
strengths: ● Functional athlete for his size and can attack vertically ● Not ﬂuid but fast and nimble enough to work himself open ● Attacks the ball with strong hands and focus, which allows him to maximize his catch radius ● Impressive play strength in the passing game, excelling through contact mid-route and at crowded catch points ● Fearless working the middle, ﬁnding soft spots and securing through traffic ● Flashes point-of-attack strength and physicality blocking inline ● Good base and upper-body pop to create movement on down blocks ● Doesn't consistently sustain but is quick to attack defenders again to keep them occupied ● Added to kick return unit senior season ● NFL scouts say his mental approach will ﬁt a pro locker room
weaknesses: ● Average quickness in and out of breaks and will stumble at times on athletic moves ● Not currently a route technician; can improve his salesmanship ● Wasn't asked to run a variety of downﬁeld routes (only two of his 43 catches in 2024 were for 25 yards or more — both came in the ﬁnal two games) ● Shows only one gear and wasn't a factor after the catch on tape ● Can slide to protect the corner but will be jolted at contact ● Battled several injuries over his high school and college careers: broken left foot during offseason workouts (July 2022), which required surgery to repair ﬁfth metatarsal and kept him out for ﬁrst ﬁve games of 2022 season; torn MCL and partially torn ACL in left knee (Oct. 2023), which forced him to miss ﬁnal four games; missed one game as junior because of a concussion (Sept. 2023) THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 161
summary: A three-year starter at Notre Dame, Evans was a versatile tight end in offensive coordinator Mike Denbrock's zone-based, run-heavy scheme, splitting his snaps between the slot (47.2 percent) and inline (42.1 percent) over his career. Despite multiple injuries that kept him from becoming a more productive weapon, he proved to be a dependable option whom the quarterback could lean on when needed. Though not particularly explosive or ﬂuid as a route runner, Evans quickly attacks open voids and has passer-friendly ball skills to consistently win through contact or come down with difficult grabs. He often went quiet in the red zone, which needs to change in the NFL (only ﬁve of his 77 career catches came inside the opponent's 20-yard line). He might not be a technician as a blocker, but he is competitive at the point of attack. Overall, Evans might not be special in any one area, but he has a well-rounded game with the tools to be a solid secondary option in an NFL passing offense. As long as he stays healthy, he can earn his way onto the ﬁeld in "12" personnel packages.

name: Jake Briningstool
strengths: ● Above-average athlete for the position with seam speed to attack vertically ● Efficient in releases to quickly enter routes ● Eats up ground as a route runner but also throttles down quickly to break off the top of stem ● Plays the ball well in the air with quick reﬂexes to adjust mid-ﬂight and contort reach ● Strong hands — one-handed grabs appear routine ● Willing to mix things up; physicality as a blocker improved each season ● Aggressive lead blocker on counters and leads, where he can build up momentum ● Durable — missed only one game over the past three seasons ● Voted a 2024 team captain THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 162
weaknesses: ● Lean build and needs to continue adding mass and strength ● Can do better job using his hips, eyes and strides get open, especially in intermediate game ● Expected more of him after the catch — isn't much of a tackle-breaking threat ● Needs to do more to avoid contact mid-route ● Maintains focus in traffic but can be outmuscled by more aggressive defenders ● Works hard at blocking technique but not a true drive blocker in the run game ● Can be uprooted and outleveraged as a blocker ● Missed one game because of injury (Nov. 2024)
summary: A two-year starter at Clemson, Briningstool was a hybrid tight end in offensive coordinator Garrett Riley's up-tempo scheme (59.3 percent of his snaps from the slot, 33.6 percent inline). He combined for 99 catches over two seasons as a starter and left Clemson as the program's all-time leader for catches by a tight end (127), breaking the mark set by Jordan Leggett. With his stride and burst to eat up ground quickly, Briningstool is an athletic route runner, and he has the tracking and ball skills to work the seam or present a large target in the red zone. He needs to continue improving his play strength as a blocker, but he is effective on the move in split zones or wham opportunities, on which he can build momentum and ﬁnish. Overall, Briningstool is a tall, lean athlete who understands how to maximize his catch radius and offers enough competitiveness as a blocker to ﬁght for playing time once on an NFL roster. He projects as an "F" tight end, similar to Josh Whyle.

name: Moliki Matavao
strengths: ● Outstanding size with strong bone structure and proportionate bulk ● Good sink in his release to quickly enter and set up routes (he loves a good sail route) ● Cleanly squares off 90-degree route turns ● Basketball background, and that hand-eye coordination translates to the catch point ● Quick to return his eyes to the pocket when he keys blitz, giving his quarterback somewhere to go ● Not a pushover with the ball — would-be tacklers will fall off him ● Loves to be aggressive as a receiver, blocker and ball carrier ● Strong base as a run blocker and consistently strains to drive/ﬁnish
weaknesses: ● Didn't put seam-stretching speed on college tape ● Exposes his chest at times at the line and needs to improve hand technique against early jams ● Little bit of a windup with his hands before engaging as a blocker ● Needs to better shift his weight to stay centered and avoid getting jolted by defensive ends ● Inconsistent adjusting to moving targets ● Only one season of adequate receiving production, including just six career touchdown catches
summary: A two-year starter at UCLA, Matavao was a ﬂex tight end in former offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy's balanced scheme (37.2 percent of his snaps in the slot, 32.3 percent inline, 30.5 percent wide). A former top recruit at Oregon, he transferred to UCLA as a junior, and his production steadily increased as a senior (71 percent of his receiving yards in 2024 came over the ﬁnal ﬁve games). Using size as a tight end is an underrated skill, and Matavao does this very well, especially at the catch point, using body quickness and natural hands to frame the football. He has the size to match up as a blocker, although he needs technique work with his hands and posture for a more sustained ﬁnish. Overall, Matavao won't wow with long speed, but he offers more as a pass catcher than his college stat line suggests and shows promise as a blocker. He can secure an NFL roster spot as a backup and work his way up from there.

name: CJ Dippre
strengths: ● Good-sized athlete with adequate speed ● Fits up his blocks with strong body positioning ● Generates pop into initial contact with ﬁrm hands ● Able to cave in down blocks to clear running room behind the tackle ● Feel for ﬁnding soft spots improved throughout the season ● Small sample, but caught the ball well with defenders crowding his air space (see 2024 Vanderbilt tape) ● Has run balance to break initial tackle ● Grew up with a powerlifting father and developed a passion for weight training in high school (wants to be a strength and conditioning coach after his playing days) ● Repped 225 pounds on the bench press 32 times at the combine (ﬁfth most by a tight end since 2000) ● Played on kick return and punt coverages all four years (529 career special teams snaps)
weaknesses: ● Late and stiff when adjusting to throws outside his frame ● Doesn't explode off the ball or at the top of routes ● Wasn't a vertical seam threat in 2024 (zero catches on one target of 20 yards or more) ● Can be slowed early and late, and his route speed won't strike fear ● Non-factor in the red zone at Alabama (zero catches inside the opponent's 20-yard line in 2023-24) ● Late to move his feet and react to inside moves on pass-pro reps ● Would like to see more ﬁnishing passion in his run blocking
summary: A two-year starter at Alabama, Dippre was a Y tight end in head coach Kalen DeBoer's run-heavy, RPO-based scheme (48.4 percent of snaps inline, 29.8 percent in the slot, 17.7 percent wide in 2024). After two seasons at Maryland, he transferred to Alabama, where he was used primarily as a blocker in the Tide's base offense (averaged 38.2 offensive snaps per game). Comfortable with his hand on the ground, Dippre has a developed feel for blocking landmarks and can create momentum to execute lead/down blocks (zero penalties in 2024). He isn't a zero as a pass catcher and has more talent than his stat line suggests (zero touchdown catches at Alabama), but he needs to be more consistent snapping breaks and ﬁnishing catches that require quick adjustments. Overall, Dippre doesn't have a true distinguishing trait as a blocker or receiver, but he is good enough in both areas to have a ﬁghting chance at a roster spot. His special teams experience will be an asset in camp.

name: Thomas Fidone II
strengths: ● Runs routes with the acceleration of a big wide receiver ● Releases cleanly and doesn't lose momentum in and out of breaks ● Adequate foot speed to stretch the seam ● Uses long arms to cast a wide net and pull in catches ● Comfortable working over the middle and taking a hit (see 2024 Indiana tape) ● Persistent effort as a move blocker ● Competitive at the point of attack and attempts to run his feet ● Played in all 25 games the past two years after injuries robbed him of his ﬁrst two college seasons
weaknesses: ● Doesn't sport ideal bulk/girth on his frame ● Lacks the base strength or core power to battle NFL defensive ends ● Too upright as a blocker and route runner ● Average separation skills, because of his straight-linish tendencies ● Wasn't enough of a factor after the catch ● Just 41.7 percent of his catches in 2024 resulted in a ﬁrst down or touchdown THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 166 ● Non-contact torn ACL in his left knee during spring practices (April 2021), which sidelined him for his ﬁrst season in Nebraska's program (played three snaps); tore ACL in his left knee again the following spring (March 2022) and missed a second straight season ● Below-average career production
summary: A two-year starter at Nebraska, Fidone was a Y tight end in former offensive coordinator Marcus Satterﬁeld's pro-style spread (61.5 percent of snaps inline, 35.1 percent in the slot). Highly recruited out of high school (ranked one spot ahead of Brock Bowers in the 2021 tight end recruiting class), his career was sidetracked by two major knee injuries, although he returned to the ﬁeld and ﬂashed that high-level ability. Fidone is at his best on a linear plane, where he can get down the seam and utilize maximum extension with his arm length to pull in throws away from his body. He is cognizant of his hands and positioning as a blocker, but he is more of a "lose slowly" player than an overwhelming force. Overall, Fidone is a plucky athlete with appealing length and speed, but he hasn't yet played his best football and will need to develop quickly once in an NFL camp to earn a role. He didn't play much special teams in college, which will need to change at the next level.

name: Jackson Hawes
strengths: ● Good-sized athlete with developed muscle on his frame ● Squares up well as a blocker and keeps his hands inside to stay attached ● Above-average balance to turn out edge defenders on front-side zone ● Works well laterally on outside zone to maintain body positioning ● Physical and persistent on down/scoop blocks ● Finishes with an intense demeanor (almost double-digit knockdowns on the 2024 Florida State tape) ● Breaks down well on the move to roll his hips into contact ● Above-average catch radius THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 167
weaknesses: ● Poor receiving production and undeveloped as a route runner ● Inefficient footwork in releases and at the top of the route, leading to wasted movements ● A tad stiff when adjusting to throws or redirecting out of breaks ● Unproven pass catcher in high-traffic situations (zero catches on two contested targets in 2024) ● Wasn't used as a red zone threat on tape (zero catches inside the opponent's 10-yard line in 2024) ● Drops his eyes at times in pass protection, losing sight of his target ● Will turn 25 during his rookie season
summary: A one-year starter at Georgia Tech, Hawes was an inline tight end in offensive coordinator Buster Faulkner's run-heavy scheme (65.0 percent of snaps inline, 28.3 percent in the slot). He spent ﬁve years at Yale and picked up an Ivy League degree before spending his ﬁnal college season with the Yellow Jackets in 2024. His performance at Georgia Tech earned him draftable grades from NFL teams. As a pass catcher, Hawes tracks and catches the ball well, but he wasn't a high-volume target in college — that is reﬂected in his inefficient route running and choppy attempts to separate at the stem. Where he shines is as a versatile, throwback blocker who can dig out defenders and stay between his target and the football. Overall, Hawes is a one-speed athlete and has a low ceiling as a passing target, but his functional athleticism, technical approach and competitive attitude should be enough to keep him on an NFL roster. He is a classic Y tight end prospect.

name: Jalin Conyers
strengths: ● Impressive athlete for his size (outstanding tester at the combine) ● Outstanding short-area quickness and balance for easy direction changes ● Versatile route tree to make plays at all three levels ● Displays coordination to position himself, elevate and adjust to catch the ball away from the defender ● Works with bodies around him — wins 50-50 balls with timing and toughness ● Can body sell and burst off his plant foot at top of the route ● Finishes with physicality and play strength as a ball carrier ● Rangy blocker to hook linebackers or cover up safeties on the move ● Effective as a wildcat option; scored three different ways in 2024; had ﬁve catches, two carries and a TD pass on the Baylor tape
weaknesses: ● Speed is more build-up than immediate ● Fluid in and out of breaks but would beneﬁt from better throttle and control in route construction ● Drops are usually a result of trying to trap/clap the football ● Inconsistent in the open ﬁeld — was hoping to see more run-after-catch work on his tape ● Has juice to make tacklers miss, but his setup is disjointed ● Solid pop as a blocker but inconsistent sustain ● Inconsistent technique hinders his ability to move bodies or anchor ● Average production; never reached 500 receiving yards in a season
summary: A one-year starter at Texas Tech, Conyers was a hybrid tight end in former offensive coordinator Zach Kittley's version of the Air Raid (55.9 percent of snaps in the slot, 34.6 percent inline/wing, 7.1 percent wide). A Red Raiders fan growing up in West Texas, he made stops at Oklahoma and Arizona State before ﬁnding his way to Lubbock for his ﬁfth season — he ﬁnished second on the team in touchdowns in 2024. Conyers has a basketball background, which shows in the quick-footed movements in his lower body and the ﬂexibility in his upper half to easily adjust at the catch point. He isn't polished as a route runner or blocker, but he can sink, and there is plenty of room for maturation in both areas. Overall, Conyers has NFL athleticism and talent. Whether or not he can ﬁne-tune the details will determine his chance of carving out a long-term role as a No. 2 TE option. He has the versatility to be ﬂexed around the ﬁeld as a steady blocker and target.

name: Gavin Bartholomew
strengths: ● Tall target with room to get stronger ● Efficient releases to avoid early contact ● Smooth linear acceleration with subtle body movements as a route runner ● Tracks the football well mid-route and has the focus to win contested windows ● Loves to stiff-arm defenders post-catch ● Functional lead blocker who gives effort through the whistle ● Stays low into engagement, creating upward strikes to neutralize at point of attack ● Team captain and positive inﬂuence in the program ● A regular on punt coverages in 2024 (one tackle)
weaknesses: ● Lighter than ideal with disproportionately short arms ● More quick than explosive in short areas ● Doesn't play with harmony between his feet and hips to sink and break off routes ● Yards per catch dropped by nearly 10 from his junior (18.1) to senior (8.5) seasons ● Needs to better use his frame to shield defenders from the ball ● Doesn't have ideal anchor for pass-pro duties ● Body control breaks down as a run blocker ● Missed ﬁnal two games of his junior season because of a high left ankle sprain (Nov. 2023)
summary: A four-year starter at Pittsburgh, Bartholomew was a wing/slot tight end in offensive coordinator Kade Bell's scheme. With Kenny Pickett at his quarterback in 2021, he put himself on the NFL radar as a freshman, although he struggled to build on that early success over the past three years (never reached 350 receiving yards in a season). Bartholomew plays with promising speed and toughness over the middle and can chew up yards versus zone, but he lacks the explosive traits to effortlessly separate from man coverage. His blocking improved incrementally each season, turning from a glaring weakness to a serviceable piece of his game — a reﬂection of his hard work and tenacious attitude. Overall, Bartholomew needs to continue getting stronger and sharpening his routes to ﬁnd a permanent home in the NFL, but he has better pass-catching traits than his stat line would suggest. His intangibles will make it tough for a coaching staff to cut him.

name: Joshua Simon
strengths: ● Decent-sized athlete with long arms to match ● Pushes off the line and creates quick catching windows ● Gliding straight-line speed and tracks the ball well in stride ● Only two drops on 90 targets during his two seasons at South Carolina ● Strong pluck-and-tuck skills; uses his length to turn incompletions into catches ● Motors like a bull and looks unfazed running through arm tackles ● Caught a touchdown every 6.2 receptions ● Shows promise in pass pro (aside from a whiff on the 2024 Kentucky tape) ● Able to create movement in the run game when he stays low and drives his legs
weaknesses: ● Frame appears near maxed out, and he can be overmatched by size at the point of attack ● Not a technician as a run blocker, especially when working inline ● Needs more reliable life in his feet once engaged, to be a better ﬁnisher ● Clunky feet in his stop-start route redirection ● Didn't put many vertical-seam routes on tape ● Fumbled ﬁve times over the past three seasons (three fumbles in 2024) ● Season-ending knee injury in the 2021 season opener ● Didn't play on special teams in 2024 ● Will turn 25 during his rookie season THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 171
summary: A two-year starter at South Carolina, Simon was a wing/slot tight end in former offensive coordinator Dowell Loggains' zone-based run scheme (heavy pre-snap motions with the tight end). He put himself on the NFL radar with his production at Western Kentucky (school record for touchdowns by a tight end) before his 2021 knee injury sidetracked things. He got back on track with the Gamecocks and set career bests in 2024, becoming the ﬁrst tight end in school history to lead the team in catches, receiving yards and touchdowns in a single season. With 87 percent of his catches in a South Carolina uniform coming within 10 yards of the line of scrimmage, Simon wasn't asked to stretch the seam. He did show his speed on drags/crossers designed to stretch out his stride and break tackles (No. 9 among FBS tight ends in yardage after the catch in 2024). As a blocker, he will get his nose dirty but needs improved technique to help compensate for his average size. Overall, Simon has explosive elements to his proﬁle, along with the ball skills and toughness that will serve him well in an NFL tight end room. He projects as a reserve F tight end.

name: Luke Lachey
strengths: ● Decent-sized frame for the position, with room for additional bulk ● Smooth athlete; transitions weight well out of breaks to create quick windows (could have played college basketball) ● Deliberate with route footwork to affect coverage (loves circus routes) ● Strong, dependable hands (only three drops on 111 career targets) ● Consistently catches the ball off his shoe tops or outside his frame ● Willing inline blocker who keeps edge defenders occupied ● Shows ﬁght after the catch and always has his eyes on the sticks ● Latches onto defenders in motion and escorts them away from the ball ● Work ethic and commitment were ingrained in him early as the youngest in a family of athletes ● Senior captain and "the same guy every day," according to NFL scouts
weaknesses: ● One-speed athlete who lacks suddenness in his movements ● Wasn't a factor downﬁeld (only four of 28 catches in 2024 came on targets of 10 yards or more) ● Occasionally gives ﬁrst defender the slip but doesn't have breakaway capabilities ● Late sifting through traffic near the line and when entering his route ● Average balance through contact as a blocker — ends up on the ground more than you'd like ● Would like to see him tighten up his blocking hands ● Broken ﬁbula in right ankle, which required season-ending surgery (Sept. 2023) and six months of rehabilitation; missed one game (and parts of others) as senior because of quad injury (Oct. 2024)
summary: A two-year starter at Iowa, Lachey was a Y tight end in offensive coordinator Tim Lester's pro-style scheme (63.8 percent of snaps inline; 29.4 percent in the slot). The top-ranked recruit in the Hawkeyes' 2020 class, he is next up in the Iowa-to-NFL pipeline, despite below-average college production caused by injuries and a listless passing offense (only one red zone catch and zero touchdowns over his ﬁnal two seasons). Strictly an underneath target in 2024, Lachey is an average speed player and more smooth than explosive, but he efficiently transfers his momentum in and out of breaks to give his quarterback a target on stick routes. Bigger defenders will give him trouble inline in the run game, but he is at his best when he can latch and drive on the move. Overall, Lachey doesn't have any dynamic elements in his game, but he catches the ball cleanly and is willing to do the dirty work in the run game. His competitive wiring will help him compete for a backup role in the NFL.

name: Caden Prieskorn
strengths: ● Prototypical size dimensions by NFL standards ● NFL-level hand-eye coordination to snare the ball away from his body ● Finishes with big, strong hands (sometimes *too* comfortable using only one hand) ● Tracks the ball beautifully down the seam and can high point when needed ● Skillfully uses his frame to out-angle defenders and lay claim to air space ● Former quarterback — shows a natural feel for route pacing ● Efficient enough to execute combo blocks and keep defenders occupied ● Mature personality and has overcome adversity (former quarterback, former walk-on, father's death, etc.)
weaknesses: ● Average speed and burst limit the ways he can separate versus man ● Not very loose at the break point ● Doesn't offer much elusiveness after the catch and will be caught from behind ● Limited hip snap as an inline blocker ● Base narrows at contact, zapping any lower-body power as a drive blocker ● Wasn't used on special teams, outside of ﬁeld goal attempts ● Will be 26 as a rookie ● Missed ﬁrst three games of his senior season because of a left foot injury, which required minor surgery (Aug. 2023)
summary: A two-year starter at Ole Miss, Prieskorn was a ﬂex tight end in offensive coordinator Charlie Weis Jr.'s spread scheme (44.1 percent of snaps in the slot, 34.3 percent inline/wing, 11.9 percent wide). An older prospect who is married with two young children, he has taken a long journey to this point — quarterback in high school and at Fork Union Military Academy, walk-on (with a position switch) at Memphis, ﬁnal stop of his college career at Ole Miss. Prieskorn doesn't have the speed to easily separate (before or after the catch), but he can be more physical than defenders at the top of routes and displays outstanding hand-eye coordination (caught 11 of 13 contested targets with the Rebels). He can cover up defenders as a blocker in the run game, too, but doesn't have the lateral agility or power to re-establish the line of scrimmage. Overall, Prieskorn is a vacuum-handed, dependable pass catcher who can be a chain-mover, but he isn't an explosive threat and has limitations to how he can impact the game. He is an easy player to like but has a low ceiling as a pro.

name: Rivaldo Fairweather
summary: Rivaldo Fairweather grew up playing different sports, but his "ﬁrst love" was basketball. He gave football a chance as a junior at Boyd Anderson High, starting out as the punter. He moved to a pass-catching role as a senior and exploded with 812 receiving yards and 15 touchdowns (also lettered in basketball, soccer and track). A three-star recruit, he was late to enter the recruiting process, but Florida International took a chance on his senior-year ﬂashes. After three productive seasons with the Panthers, he joined Auburn for his ﬁnal two college seasons. Still a relatively unpolished player, Fairweather does a nice job with blocking angles to shield defensive ends from the ball, but he needs to be more consistent executing second-level blocks. He was very effective blocking for a two count before releasing as a target, showing his natural body control to easily adjust to errant throws. Overall, Fairweather doesn't create as much as I was hoping after the catch, but he is athletic at the catch point and has upside as a blocker that will interest NFL teams.

name: Robbie Ouzts
summary: Robbie Ouzts (OOTS) grew up playing sports in Rock Hill, S.C., and developed a love for football, because of the physicality. His favorite player growing up was fullback Brad Hoover (which is why Ouzts wears No. 45). He was a fullback/tight end at Rock Hill High and posted 465 receiving yards as a senior. A three-star recruit, Ouzts committed to Alabama over other SEC programs and played a variety of roles, from aligning in the I-formation under Bill O'Brien to the "H" tight end position in Kalen DeBoer's scheme. With his trademark mustache, he has always been wired to be the hammer and not the nail — he plays with immense pride in laying out his body on every play and ﬁnishing his block by whatever means necessary. He saw just 21 career targets but showed good hands and body control when he got chances (also played 537 snaps on special teams). Overall, Ouzts is a throwback player with a gladiator mentality. He would have more opportunities in NFL offenses of 30 years ago, but he has a chance to make a roster as an H-back "sniffer" and goal line tight end.

name: Benjamin Yurosek
summary: Benjamin Yurosek, one of ﬁve children, grew up in Bakersﬁeld, Calif., and both his parents (Derek and Kellie) were athletes at Colorado State. Yurosek was an all-state tight end and defensive end at Bakersﬁeld Christian High. As a senior, he led the team to its ﬁrst state title. A three-star recruit, Yurosek committed to Stanford over Washington and was a productive pass-catching tight end. After missing half of his 2023 season, he jumped in the transfer portal and landed at Georgia, hoping to help ﬁll the void left by Brock Bowers. Instead, he was used more as a blocker in 2024 (just 20 targets in 14 games). Yurosek didn't back down when asked to get his nose dirty as an inline blocker and executed well on the move (leads, screens, etc.). He tracks the ball well mid-route, with the body control to adjust, although I wanted more out of him on red zone snaps (only two career red zone touchdowns). Overall, Yurosek doesn't have the type of exceptional size or power that will stand out on an NFL ﬁeld, but he is assignment sound and a good enough athlete. He can make an NFL roster with continued ﬁne-tuning of his run-blocking technique.

name: Brant Kuithe
summary: Brant Kuithe (keeth-ee), whose twin brother (Blake) also played at Utah, grew up outside of Houston with his parents (Dennis and Debbie). He started playing football in grade school (on the offensive line) and grew into a do-everything weapon (including punting) at Cinco Ranch High. As a senior, he rushed for more than 1,000 yards in seven games and was named district MVP. THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 176 A three-star recruit, Kuithe made an immediate impact for the Utes as a hybrid tight end and received draftable grades from NFL scouts. But he suffered a torn ACL (Sept. 2022), which required multiple surgeries — the setbacks kept him sidelined for 2023, as well. He returned in 2024, only to suffer another season-ending injury. When healthy, Kuithe is an NFL-caliber athlete and a matchup weapon out of the slot. He stems and creates separation, especially on in-breakers, which also gives him a chance to show off his YAC talent. He is a more physical blocker than one might expect, but he will always be limited by his size. Overall, Kuithe has draftable talent with the athletic versatility and pass-catching ability to help an offense and play special teams. His durability, though, is the chief concern.

name: Bryson Nesbit
strengths: ● Not explosive but has practical speed down the seam (better than his timed speed would suggest) ● Natural coordination when adjusting to imprecise passes ● Workable catch radius to spear the ball, despite average arm length ● Efficient outside-in breaks to cross the face of coverage THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 177 ● Can sink pad level into his stem to plant and break off route ● Decent job as a move blocker on split-zone ● Grew up around the New Orleans Saints' locker room and knows what to expect from NFL life
weaknesses: ● Light in his lower half, with lean muscle tone ● Can be dominated at the point of attack as a play-side blocker ● Wide, wild hands with initial engagement and struggles to stay latched ● Rarely used in pass protection on 2024 tape ● Battled focus lapses, which led to drops on almost every tape studied ● Not sudden or twitchy in his movements, limiting his separation before and after the catch ● Want to see better physicality from him mid-route ● Final two seasons were marred by injuries: played through a partially torn meniscus in his left knee (Nov. 2023) over the ﬁnal month of the regular season before undergoing surgery (Dec. 2023), which sidelined him for 2024 spring practices; fractured wrist (Oct. 2024), which required surgery and sidelined him for the ﬁnal ﬁve games
summary: A part-time starter at North Carolina, Nesbit was a "joker" tight end in former offensive coordinator Chip Lindsey's spread pro scheme (80.1 percent of his 2024 snaps came in the slot). He didn't start playing football until his junior year of high school but quickly put himself on the NFL map while catching passes from Drake Maye, before injuries disrupted his ﬁnal two seasons. Nesbit has functional athletic traits in his routes and at the catch point, but his NFL paycheck will depend on his receiving impact — he needs to play stronger through contact and button up his catch-point focus. Though he ﬂashed promise as a move blocker in college, he consistently punches below his weight class with below-average sustain/ﬁnish strength. Overall, Nesbit has silky adjustment skills and is more of a large-framed wide receiver than traditional tight end.
