summary: A three-year starter at Ohio State, Tuimoloau played on the edge in former defensive coordinator Jim Knowles' four-man front, primarily in a two-point crouched stance. The highest-ranked recruit ever to sign in Columbus, he never reached the Bosa brothers or Chase Young level of pass rusher for the Buckeyes, but his ﬂashes evolved into consistent production, and he played the best ball of his career during Ohio State's four College Football Playoff games in 2024 (20 pressures, 10 tackles for loss, 6.5 sacks, one forced fumble). A ﬂexible, long athlete, Tuimoloau creates lift and extension through contact and uses his football GPS and short-area agility to close on the ball carrier. He frequently saw four hands as a pass rusher (opponents knew he was the main threat on a talented Buckeyes defensive line), but he needs to develop more seamless counter sequencing when left one-on-one on the edge. He has a terriﬁc motor and should continue developing his shed timing to improve his run ﬁts. Overall, Tuimoloau's college tape is more good than exceptional, but he is competitive, skilled and doesn't have major deﬁciencies that would keep him from being a dependable edge presence in the NFL. He is one of the most well-rounded defensive prospects in the class.

summary: A three-year starter at Arkansas, Jackson was the "Buck" end in defensive coordinator Travis Williams' four-man front (94.6 percent of his snaps in 2024 came over or outside of the offensive tackle). THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 295 Using more of a "jet mode" stance as a super senior, Kennard was able to improve his takeoff as a pass rusher to be disruptive from wide alignment. He can use his length in different ways to pry open blocks, but he is inconsistent as a point-of-attack player and larger tackles can engulf him. Overall, Kennard has work to do developing his counters and becoming more consistent on run downs to reach his NFL potential, but he brings energetic speed off the edge when he can pin his ears back. He projects as a passing-down specialist, and his role can evolve from there.

name: Elijah Roberts
strengths: ● Average height, but a wide, thick build and long arms ● Plays with brute strength and force in his hands to jar at contact ● Well-executed speed-to-power moves, using both hands to drive/forklift blockers ● Shows natural feel for hesitation/stutter bulls ● Has lateral agility for inside swipes and chop-cross moves ● Above-average run awareness and quickly reads blocking schemes ● Doesn't allow length go to waste; uses different lock-out techniques to set the edge ● Drops his weight into pullers to create immediate stopping power ● Senior captain and competes with a hungry motor ● Posted consistent backﬁeld production past two seasons THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 296
weaknesses: ● Average initial burst, with stiffness in his hips and ankles ● Doesn't have lower-body ﬂexibility to easily dip or turn the corner against NFL tackles ● Pass-rush movements tend to be segmented and forecasted at times ● Undeveloped countering technique ● Left too much tackle production on the ﬁeld on 2024 tape ● Doesn't offer much in reverse; unproven lining up inside the tackle ● Missed one game as a super senior because of a broken bone in right hand (Nov. 2024) — wore a thick cast ﬁnal four games
summary: A two-year starter at SMU, Roberts lined up primarily as an edge rusher (seven-/nine-technique) in defensive coordinator Scott Symons four-man base line. He struggled to ﬁnd a consistent role in three years at Miami, but he ﬂourished with the Mustangs and combined for 131 pressures over the past two seasons (No. 1 in the FBS over that span). Roberts has a very unique body type for an edge rusher, but he knows how to affect the quarterback by leaning into his strengths — speciﬁcally, his long arms and ability to create force at contact (especially if the blocker plays with wide hands and invites Roberts' signature bull rush into his chest). He drops his weight against the run, locks out and holds his own at the point of attack, although his range was inconsistent when working off contact. Overall, Roberts is more deliberate than dynamic as an athlete. He accelerates well in short areas, though, and power is the foundation of his game, which shows both as a pass rusher and edge setter. His uniqueness might scare off some teams, but he has the goods to be a rotational edge with upside on the interior.

name: Fadil Diggs
strengths: ● Prototypical dimensions with his frame, length and hand size ● Quality athlete in his footwork and moves well in space for his size ● Better bend and ﬂexibility than expected for a player that long ● Syracuse weaponized his downhill burst and physicality as A-gap blitzer from depth ● Nifty inside arm-over move to create a rush lane ● Solid understanding of how to ﬁt the run from stacked position ● Physical mentality — will throw his shoulder into contact to clog lanes or stone pulling linemen ● Twice named a team captain at Texas A&M and ingrained himself quickly in Syracuse culture in 2024 ● Set career bests in backﬁeld production in 2024
weaknesses: ● Average get-off by NFL standards ● Segmented pass rush; not a polished technician ● Can get hung up on blocks when attempting to work off initial strike ● Powerful blockers can break down his anchor and shield him from lanes ● Streaky break down and ﬁnish as tackler, leading to misses (see 2024 Ohio tape) ● Had more than 100 coverage reps in 2024 but didn't look natural ﬁnding passing lanes ● Missed ﬁnal four games of sophomore season because of lower-body injury (Oct. 2022); missed bowl game as senior because of lower-body injury (Dec. 2024)
summary: A one-year starter at Syracuse, Diggs was an edge rusher in defensive coordinator Elijah Robinson's four-man front, often standing up on sub-package downs and rushing from different angles (28.3 percent of his 2024 defensive snaps came in the box). After four seasons in College Station, he followed Elijah Robinson to Syracuse and led the team in tackles for loss (14) and sacks (7.5) in 2024. Although his rush attack is a tad predictable, Diggs is a long strider who can eat up ground with a runway and unleash his heavy hands to bulldoze at contact. His inconsistent pad level and lock-out needs work as an edge setter, but he doesn't shy from contact. Overall, Diggs might not have any exceptional traits that separate him, but he is a well-rounded player with enough athleticism and physicality packed into an NFL frame. He projects as a scheme-versatile NFL backup who can provide a nice changeup off the bench.

name: Jared Ivey
strengths: ● NFL-ready frame with functional length/bulk ● Uses long-levered extension to jolt and work off contact ● Leans on various physical swipes to slice the edge with his hands ● Times snap well with lateral agility to jump cut inside/outside ● Consistently rallying to the football to make stops away from his spot ● Can set the edge when he locks out with strain to stay rooted ● Former coaches always bring up his intelligence before physical traits ● Developed love for the weight room to build up body (195 pounds as a high school junior) ● Charismatic and jells well in locker room (also hosted podcast at Ole Miss called "Ivey League")
weaknesses: ● Rushes tall, creating a big target for hands of blockers ● Euro steps and move timing feel rigid at times ● Will drift past the quarterback on high-side rushes ● Can stack, but his shed and secondary quickness off contact lack suddenness ● Plays with competitive edge on some plays — but not every play ● Can be juked by average athletes in backﬁeld ● Missed one game as super senior with left foot injury (Sept. 2024)
summary: A three-year starter at Ole Miss, Ivey lined up primarily on the edge (seven-/nine-technique) in defensive coordinator Pete Golding's 4-2-5 base scheme after splitting his snaps 50-50 inside and outside in 2023. After two losing seasons at Georgia Tech, he transferred to greener pastures in Oxford and logged 16 sacks in a Rebels uniform, which ranks top 10 in program history. Though not twitchy, Ivey is a graceful athlete for his size, with a basketball background and length for days, which helps him set an edge, spill and chase in the run game. He rolls out of his stance as a pass rusher to build his speed and get his hands involved, but he lacks a consistent plan and struggles to string moves together. Overall, Ivey has the length and versatile skill set NFL teams want in their defensive line rooms, although he needs to play with more consistent violence and rush efficiency to stand out when working alongside proven NFL vets. He can contribute on sub-package downs as a rookie and push for a more meaningful role with added consistency.

name: Jah Joyner
strengths: ● Passes the eye test with a long, moldable frame ● Quality athlete who moves well laterally and linearly ● Quick off the ball and gains ground with initial step ● Arsenal of moves expanded as senior, including ghost rip that became effective for him ● Closes fast to the ball and makes plays in backside pursuit ● Shows functional core strength to constrict the edge ● Did a better job maximizing length when setting the edge in 2024 ● Uses his long arms to bat down balls at the line ● Came in at 220 pounds and developed his body over the years ● Coaches speak about his maturity and how he grew to be more of a vocal guy in the room
weaknesses: ● Not as powerful as expected (even with a runway), and his bull rush can be neutralized ● Inconsistent setup and pass-rush disguise ● Needs to think less and be more efficient with move-to-move rush sequence ● Finds himself too upright versus the run, with average reaction quickness ● Takes a beat to digest what he sees — needs to be more instant off spots ● Some undisciplined tendencies (two facemask penalties on 2024 tapes studied) ● Just 13 starts over ﬁve years at the college level ● Sack and pressure numbers decreased from 2023 to 2024, despite playing more snaps
summary: A one-year starter at Minnesota, Joyner lined up primarily as an outside edge rusher in defensive coordinator Corey Hetherman's four-man front. He was slow to see the ﬁeld (played behind NFL Draft picks Boye Mafe and Esezi Otomewo) before showing NFL promise in 2023 and improvements in 2024, despite a production dip the latter year. THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 300 A long-framed athlete, Joyner looks the part and does a nice job using his length at the point of attack to set the edge and ﬁnish as a tackler. His long strides and levers are assets for him as a pass rusher, as well, but he is too predictable in his attack and needs to develop his sequencing and balance at the top of his rush. Overall, Joyner has impressive physical attributes, with the toolbox that NFL coaches want to work with, but he is still learning the ﬁner points of the pass rush and his impact doesn't currently reﬂect his traits. He has the upside of an NFL starter, but his tape shows a rotational player — until he proves otherwise.

name: Antwaun Powell-Ryland
strengths: ● Varies rush attack to keep blockers on their toes ● Looks to threaten with speed, force over sets and hit blockers with a counter spin ● Flexibility in lower half as a high-side rusher ● Nice timing with his hands and leverage mechanics to convert speed to power at contact ● Almost half (44.2 percent) of his tackles in 2024 came in opponent's backﬁeld ● Chases in the run game and quickly digests play development ● Has a knack for ripping the football out (nine forced fumbles over past three seasons) ● Blocked extra point attempt on 2024 Syracuse tape THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 301
weaknesses: ● A tad lighter than ideal for edge work, with below-average arm length ● Functional strength was okay against ACC competition but will be a potential issue versus NFL blocking power ● Average burst at the line ● Inconsistent working back under once past pocket depth ● Tackles high and looks to throw ball carriers down, which leads to misses (see 2024 Boston College tape) ● Not a player you want dropping into space ● Stayed healthy in college but had multiple shoulder procedures in high school
summary: A two-year starter at Virginia Tech, Powell-Ryland was an edge rusher in head coach Brent Pry's four-man front, lining up exclusively outside the tackle on both base and sub downs. Primarily a reserve over his three seasons at Florida, he transferred back home and led the FBS in sacks over the past two seasons (25.5). He registered four sacks three different times for the Hokies, joining Bruce Smith as the only players in school history with multiple four-sack games. Despite below-average length and get-off burst, Powell-Ryland was a difficult player to block on tape, because of his ability to mix up his rush attack and detach from blockers (including his signature spin move). He can get pushed around as a run defender when setting an edge, and he might not be ready for early-down snaps in the NFL until he improves his upper- and lower-body strength. Overall, Powell-Ryland posted eye-popping pass-rush production with active hands to slip blocks, but he doesn't offer ideal traits by NFL standards and inconsistent run-game reps leave his NFL role in question. He projects as a potential nickel rusher.

name: Que Robinson
strengths: ● Tall, athletic frame with adequate length ● Flashes get-off and bend ● Lower-body ﬂexibility helps him sink, redirect and make tackles in short spaces ● Eager with his hands to physically escape blockers ● Striding speed helps him close alleys and chase down ball carriers ● Can drop and spy or rush over B-gap ● Described as "mature and humble" ● Core-four special-teamer and an impact performer past three seasons (15 career special teams tackles)
weaknesses: ● Slender for the position and lacks ideal mass ● Blockers can get leverage wins against him ● Needs to school up his hands to help compensate for average strength ● Late to anticipate blocks in the run game, losing sight of the ball in traffic ● Undeveloped pass-rush arsenal ● Just ﬁve starts in college — lack of experience is reﬂected on tape ● Career production wouldn't be impressive in just one season for a pass rusher ● Missed ﬁnal four games of his ﬁnal season with an elbow injury (Nov. 2024)
summary: A part-time starter at Alabama, Robinson played the "Wolf" edge position in defensive coordinator Kane Womack's hybrid front. Buried on the depth chart in Tuscaloosa, he saw just 370 defensive snaps in college, resulting in 5.5 career sacks (just 1.5 against SEC competition). Though he struggled to make an impact on defense, Robinson made the most of his playing time by becoming a key special teams performer across all four coverages. He ﬂashes range as a run defender and short-area quickness as a pass rusher, but he needs to replace his hands consistently on his get-off and become comfortable countering once initially blocked. Overall, Robinson is a traits-based, tweener prospect with potential as an edge setter, although his lack of development is going to stick out like a sore thumb next to NFL players in training camp. His saving grace is his coverage talent on special teams, which might keep him on a roster as he grows as a defender.

name: Kaimon Rucker
strengths: ● Compact, well-proportioned build with strong legs ● Quick off the ball and creates force with initial acceleration ● Natural leverage and body strength don't allow blockers to push him off rush track ● Efficiently toggles between burst and hesitation to weaponize rush pace through soft edges ● Unleashes hand swipe and rip move at the top of the rush ● Keeps outside arm free and maintains block-to-ball contain relationships ● Patient reads; eyes trained on the football help him make run stops at the line ● Prides himself on setting a standard by outworking the guy next to him (head coach Mack Brown: "He's smart, tough and driven.") ● Coaches relied on his leadership (former defensive coordinator Geoff Collins: "He knows which buttons to push.") ● His career total of 22 sacks ranks No. 6 all-time in Tar Heels history
weaknesses: ● Lacks ideal height and length by NFL standards ● Mediocre ﬂuidity doesn't help secondary rush moves ● Controlling blocks against NFL offensive tackles won't be a walk in the park ● Hand activity helps keep him free, but he will be moved from his spot when he loses leverage ● Inconsistent reactions handling pullers in run game ● Doesn't have chase-down speed to close the gap in pursuit ● Rarely asked to drop and make plays in space (did have an interception on the 2024 Virginia tape) ● Cracked ﬁbula after an NC State offensive lineman rolled on his left leg (Nov. 2024), which sidelined him for bowl game and part of draft process; reaggravated previous knee injury while lifting weights (Sept. 2024) and required a cleanup procedure to repair a torn meniscus, which sidelined him four games; ruptured tendon in right middle ﬁnger (Nov. 2023) — played through it over ﬁnal two games before getting offseason surgery (April 2024), which sidelined him for spring practices
summary: A four-year starter at North Carolina, Rucker lined up as the "Rush" end in former defensive coordinator Geoff Collins' four-man front (100 percent of his defensive snaps in 2024 came outside the offensive tackle). Although his super-senior season didn't go as planned because of injuries, his value was never more apparent — the energy on North Carolina's defense was like night and day when he was sidelined or on the ﬁeld. Rucker, who received the nickname "The Butcher" after former defensive line coach Tim Cross described him as a "rolling ball of butcher knives," is an explosive linear athlete and attacks the hips of blockers to win with natural leverage. He can be covered up at times in the run game, but his discipline and fast, physical hands help him punch off blocks. Overall, Rucker doesn't have the high-level rush tools to make teams easily overlook his size deﬁciencies, but he plays with violent energy that gives him a chance to carve out a role. His game resembles that of Ogbo Okoronkwo, who has been a productive NFL pass rusher.

name: Tyler Baron
strengths: ● Tall with decent mass and arm length ● Good ﬁrst step to build speed and challenge the corner ● Adequate bend to dip, rip and straighten out to the quarterback ● Aggressive hands — uses a variety of cross-chops and stab-rips ● Can keep blockers off him when he properly uses length and keeps his feet alive ● Average quickness to cross the face of blockers and threaten inside gaps ● Plays with quality hustle as a pursuit player ● Learned from Hall of Famer (Jason Taylor) as defensive ends coach in 2024 THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 305
weaknesses: ● Streaky competitor with ordinary play strength ● Undisciplined on zone-read assignments ● Caught leaning on blocks as edge setter, instead of consistently locking out ● Pad level gets up and down, which gets him in trouble ● Doesn't protect his chest and can be knocked off path easily ● Finds himself too deep at times as a rusher ● Too many penalties, including a roughing penalty on 2024 Florida State tape ● Left too much tackle production on 2024 tape ● Loses track of targets when spot dropping in coverage ● Missed 2024 spring practices because of labrum surgery
summary: A one-year starter at Miami, Baron was an outside edge rusher (seven-/nine-technique) in former defensive coordinator Lance Guidry's four-man front. Considered a transfer-portal prize for the Hurricanes, he didn't quite live up to expectations in 2024, although he did lead Miami in tackles for loss, pressures and sacks (even if three of his 5.5 sacks came versus an FCS team). Baron is a charged-up linear athlete who has some tightness but can dip and escape blocks when his hand timing stays on point. Though he has a solid pursuit motor, the inconsistent physicality and discipline at the point of attack was a consistent issue on tape. Overall, Baron has some pass-rush skill, but he's an uneven run performer and there isn't much that distinguishes him by NFL standards, beyond being a potential rotational piece. If he brings his fastball, he is a potential sub-package rusher for an NFL defense.

name: Ahmed Hassanein
strengths: ● Owns a compact, developed frame ● Blockers can have a tough time with his motor ● Hands are small but ﬂash violence at contact ● Promising skill as a rusher — has shown key improvements the last few seasons ● Leverages point of attack to set a physical edge ● Voted a team captain in 2024 and genuinely loves to train with his teammates, whom he refers to as his "brothers" ● Tough as nails — played through a torn labrum (Oct. 2023) over ﬁnal nine games of his junior season (10 sacks in that span) ● Consistent production — only FBS defensive lineman to eclipse 15 tackles for loss each of past two seasons
weaknesses: ● Arms fall below desired size measurements ● Average athleticism as a rusher and in open ﬁeld ● One-speed rusher and will struggle to win the corner versus NFL offensive tackles ● Inconsistent snap anticipation and stiff when attempting to transition and ﬁnd counter ● Multiple missed tackles on several 2024 tapes studied ● Inconsistent playing through lateral engagements ● Plays in overdrive, taking himself out of run plays at times ● Didn't register a single batted pass in career and doesn't have versatility to play in reverse
summary: A two-year starter at Boise State, Hassanein was a defensive end (ﬁve-/seven-technique) in defensive coordinator Erik Chinander's 4-2-5 base scheme. After growing up in Cairo (top-ranked CrossFit athlete in Egypt as a teenager), he moved to the United States in 2018, started playing football in 2019 and became the ﬁrst player from Egypt to ever play FBS football. Hassanein is an easy player to appreciate, because he is productive (115 pressures over the past two seasons were third most in the FBS over that span) and his nonstop motor stresses blockers. However, his run-game awareness and immature pass-rush sequencing are underdeveloped. The missed tackles are bothersome, too. Overall, Hassanein is a try-hard edge rusher with plenty of redeeming qualities that will endear him to coaches. He lacks high-level athletic traits, though, and will be low on an NFL depth chart until he improves his predictability as a pass rusher. Given his meager football experience, NFL teams are intrigued by his untapped upside.

name: Elijah Ponder
summary: Elijah Ponder was born and raised in Southern California and was introduced to football by his father (also grew up playing instruments, including the piano, guitar and drums). At Bishop Amat High, he played basketball and track (school-record 47-foot triple jump) and was a do-everything athlete on the football ﬁeld. He totaled 21 sacks over his ﬁnal two years. A two-star recruit, he bypassed a few FBS offers (Colorado State, San Jose State) to sign with FCS Cal Poly. Ponder played a hybrid edge role throughout college, both standing up and putting his hand in the dirt, and ranks third in school history with 26.5 career sacks. Quick off the ball, he can threaten the corner or work across the faces of blockers inside. He uses his hands well to disrupt blockers' balance, although he needs to do a better job with angles in the run game. Overall, Ponder doesn't always play up to his testing numbers, but he rushes with an initial and late burst to affect the quarterback. He projects as a sub-package rusher.

name: Ethan Downs
strengths: ● Springs out of stance with oomph to keep blockers on their toes ● Able to beat blockers with quickness when attacking inside gaps ● Large, heavy hands to stack and shed ● Works hard to maintain his gap and pursuit leverage in the run game ● Chases with a head of steam to make effort plays in pursuit ● "Most mature and generous guy on campus," according to a Sooners assistant coach ● Tough — consistently plays through minor injuries (missed one game past four years) ● Ran routes and caught passes for NFL scouts at Oklahoma's Pro Day THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 308
weaknesses: ● Sawed-off arms and can be jolted by long-armed blockers ● Below-average ﬂexibility and gives blockers a target at the top of his rush ● Better pass-rush effort than pass-rush instincts ● Current set of counters will be ineffective against NFL tackles ● Can get washed when he gets tall out of his stance ● Outstanding hustle but gets out of control at times, leading to missed tackles ● Wasn't asked to drop much
summary: A three-year starter at Oklahoma, Downs lined up at defensive end in defensive coordinator Zac Alley's 4-2-5 base scheme. A diehard Sooner for as long as he can remember, he put himself on the NFL radar as a sophomore. Although his production dipped slightly the past two seasons, his impact showed on each tape studied. Downs is gap sound, alert and disciplined in the run game and stacks a ton of effort plays. His tape doesn't show a consistent pass-rush threat, mostly because of his lack of bend and length, but he has the quickness to work half-a-man and his physical hands help him work off blocks. Overall, Downs has some tweener traits and will be caught in between positions for several schemes, but he is a high-motor, blue-collar base end, and coaches will appreciate that they'll know exactly what they are getting every down. His experience on special teams (382 snaps in college) can help him earn a backup role

name: Tyler Batty
strengths: ● Good-sized athlete with functional build and arm length ● Comes off ball with bend and pad level, setting the table for variety of rush techniques ● Functional ankle ﬂexion for tight cornering off jab/Euro steps ● Hand swipes are punctual and married to his footwork ● Physical at point of attack to get into frame of blockers and create movement ● Promising hand-to-hand combat to establish leverage as an edge setter ● His default setting is "relentless" ● Team captain and sets the bar high for himself ● Passionate about football and stubbornly determined (Kilani Sitake: "You can count on him to be one of the hardest working guys on the team") ● Experienced college resume (45 career starts)
weaknesses: ● More worker bee than twitched-up edge screamer ● NFL offensive tackles will pick up on his rush plan much more quickly than college blockers ● Needs to continue developing shed techniques to better unglue once blockers access his chest ● Occasionally trapped by reach blocks ● Left too much tackle production on the ﬁeld ● Only 1.5 sacks in 2024 ● Torn ear, which required stitches but didn't cause him to miss any time (Oct. 2024); missed one game with an abdominal strain (Sept. 2022); sidelined most of his ﬁrst season with an ankle injury (Sept. 2020) and took a redshirt ● Will be 26 as a rookie
summary: A four-year starter at BYU, Batty lined up mostly as a ﬁve-/seven-technique in defensive coordinator Jay Hill's multiple fronts, also standing up at times or kicking inside to a 4i-technique. An older prospect who's already married, he established himself as one of the leaders in the Cougars' program, and his persistent play personality set the tempo for the rest of the defense. Although his pass rush doesn't consistently jump off the screen, Batty has a versatile play style with the ﬂexibility to work around blocks or the heavy hands to win with speed to power. He ﬂashes the potential to weaponize his hands/length as an edge setter and block shedder, although he needs to do it on a more regular basis to stay on an NFL ﬁeld. Overall, Batty might not bring the impact consistency NFL teams want in a starter or high-end backup, but he wins in different ways — defensive coordinators who place premiums on size and motor will welcome him with open arms. He can be a day one depth player.

name: Steve Linton
strengths: ● Owns a long, rangy frame and plays with energy ● Quick, both laterally and up the ﬁeld, to get around the noise ● Get-off speed will put blockers on their heels early (see 2024 Colorado tape) ● Will mix in outside jab steps to wrap shoulders of blockers ● Active hand swipes to stay off blocks ● Nimble feet in the run game with pop in his hands to widen, contain and detach ● Long strides help him close on the ball carrier when chasing ● Still has some upside as he continues to learn how to use his length
weaknesses: ● Lean-muscled and has struggled to add consistent bulk ● High cut with inconsistent dip when turning the corner ● Doesn't have power in his upper half to consistently go through blocks ● Narrow-based edge setter — can be overwhelmed in the run game ● Late to calm his feet and misses too many tackles when he plays too hot ● Multiple offsides and late hit ﬂags on tape ● Struggled to stay on the ﬁeld — long list of nagging injuries ● Will be 25 on draft weekend
summary: A one-year starter at Baylor, Linton was a wide edge rusher in head coach Dave Aranda's four-man front, lining up mostly in a two-point stance. After playing a 4i-technique at Syracuse, he moved to a more natural seven-/nine-technique role at Texas Tech in 2023 and Baylor in 2024, ﬂashing disruptive ability as a sub-package defender (averaged 33.2 defensive snaps per game over the past three seasons). Linton is long-limbed and quickly attacks the arc, but he is overly reliant on his speed and doesn't have a deep toolbox as a pass rusher, despite being a sixth-year prospect. Although he can occasionally use his length to stay detached in the run game, his strength breaks down at the point of attack and teams know they can ﬁnd success running to his side of the ﬁeld. Overall, Linton is one-dimensional and hasn't proven himself beyond being a ﬂash pass rusher, but his ﬁrst-step explosion and body length will earn him extended looks. He projects as a designated rusher on sub-downs (if he can stay healthy), in the mold of Arden Key.

name: Johnny Walker Jr.
summary: Johnny Walker Jr. grew up in Tampa, Fla., with his parents (April and Johnny Walker Sr.). At Chamberlain High, he combined for 41 tackles for loss and 25 sacks over his junior and senior seasons, despite battling a knee issue in 2019. A three-star recruit, he initially committed to Washington State before ﬂipping to Missouri late in the process. Walker bided his time before becoming a starter as a junior and earning second-team All-SEC honors as a senior captain. After recording just one sack over the ﬁrst six games of 2024, he ripped off 8.5 sacks in the ﬁnal seven. Walker has improved year over year as he's learned how to maximize his skill set. He doesn't have top-tier burst or redirect skills for a 250-pound edge rusher, but he is a better football player than a high-end athlete. He keeps his hands and feet in sync and understands how to leverage his pass-rush angles. His run-game awareness also showed improvement from his junior tape. Overall, Walker doesn't play with consistent explosion or bend, but he can dip and rip to affect the quarterback when he times up the snap. He is a potential sub-package rusher in the NFL.

name: Chaz Chambliss
summary: Charles "Chaz" Chambliss (cham-bliss) grew up with his parents (Cliff and Angela) and started playing football at age 5. His father, who spent two decades as a U.S. Army drill sergeant, died of a stroke at age 53 (March 2020). At Carrollton High, Chambliss combined for a career 251 tackles and 31.5 sacks. A four-star recruit, he committed to Georgia and bounced between inside linebacker and the Jack outside linebacker position. He saved his best for last, posting career-best numbers as a senior in 2024, including a team-high 6.5 sacks. Compactly built, Chambliss has tweener size and length, but he plays with the physicality in the run game to control the point of attack and string out runs. He makes himself a small target for blockers and uses his ﬂexibility to maneuver his body around the trees. His chase speed stands out, he doesn't miss tackles and his teammates say he's the toughest guy on the team. Overall, Chambliss is a sawed-off edge defender who can provide depth as an outside linebacker in a 3-4, but his ticket to an NFL roster spot will be as a special teams ace.

name: RJ Oben
strengths: ● Athletic frame with workable arm length ● Functional short-area quickness when working off the edge ● Flashes violent swipes/chops when attacking the corner ● Physical hands to control tight ends at point of attack ● Gap-sound in the run game to force runners laterally ● Feel for ﬁnding the football ● Younger for a sixth-year senior (started kindergarten one year early) ● Grew up around the game — won't be any surprises for him about what it takes to make it in the NFL
weaknesses: ● Below-average tackle and backﬁeld production, especially in 2024 ● Tight-hipped with inconsistent lower-body bend ● Needs to add more ammo to pass-rush arsenal ● Ineffective speed-to-power techniques ● Pads elevate off the snap, and he immediately surrenders point-of-attack leverage ● Wild play style leads to more missed tackles than acceptable ● Missed most of his ﬁrst season with a left shoulder injury, which required surgery (Oct. 2019)
summary: A one-year starter at Notre Dame, Oben was a ﬁeld edge rusher in former defensive coordinator Al Golden's four-man front. While averaging just 25 defensive snaps per game in 2024, he struggled to make a memorable impact throughout much of the season. However, he had his best performance in an Irish uniform during a playoff game against Georgia and ﬂashed during Senior Bowl week. As a pass rusher, Oben is more of an "everything but the kitchen sink" type than a crafty artist. He plays with strong hands and a radar for the football in the run game, but he will get pinballed by base blocks when he pops upright at contact. Overall, Oben is an inefficient player, but he offers a consistent football-playing temperament and tools that can be further developed. He is a potential practice squad project for a defensive staff.

name: J.J. Weaver
strengths: ● Workable frame, build and length for the position ● Loose-jointed with ﬂexibility in long limbs ● Some twitch in his upper half and uses full extension ● Active on ET stunts, creating holding penalties ● Rangy tackler and has some burst in his close ● Comfortable on his feet to spot drop and cover short zones ● Just the third three-time captain in school history ● Hard worker, in and out of the building, with strong character feedback
weaknesses: ● Poor contact balance and can be knocked off rush path too easily ● Initial rush moves are uninspiring ● Inconsistent anchor strength and ability as an edge setter ● Needs to crank up violence in his shed hands ● Tunnel vision and too easily caught up in the wash THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 314 ● Torn ACL in right knee in ﬁrst career start (Nov. 2020), which required season-ending surgery; missed two games as junior because of left elbow injury (Sept. 2022); missed two games as super senior because of ankle injury (Oct. 2024) ● Will turn 26 as a rookie (turned 19 during his senior year of high school)
summary: A four-year starter at Kentucky, Weaver was primarily a stand-up edge rusher in defensive coordinator Brad White's 3-4 base scheme. Possessing one of the more unique backgrounds in this class (has 11 ﬁngers, off-ﬁeld work, etc.), he didn't quite live up to the promise he showed on the ﬁeld as an underclassman, but he was a steady contributor for the Wildcats. Weaver is a worker-bee defender who works to get off blocks and make plays. Despite being an older player, there is still some upside there, if he improves some of the technical parts of his game, including improved leverage points as a rusher to fully access his power. Overall, Weaver has athletic and physical tools to work with at the next level, but his below-average contact balance and rush instincts will be tough to overcome against NFL competition.

name: Kydran Jenkins
summary: Kydran (KAY-dran) Jenkins, one of four children, grew up outside of Augusta, Ga., with his mother (Lisa Valles). He was a running back and linebacker at Jefferson County High, where he earned all-conference honors as a senior (83 tackles and seven forced fumbles). A three-star recruit, he received two then-Power 5 offers (Purdue and Missouri), and he committed to the Boilermakers. He primarily played as an edge rusher in college before moving to stand-up linebacker in 2024. The shift helped show his versatility, but he was still at his best when attacking the pocket. While starting all 38 games the last three seasons, he became the ﬁrst Purdue player since Ryan Kerrigan to lead the team in tackles for loss three straight seasons. Despite having shorter arms, Jenkins uses his ﬁerce hands to rid himself of blocks and make a beeline to the football. He doesn't have the tape of a playmaker in coverage, but he looks comfortable dropping and chasing. Overall, Jenkins is a force player who can work off contact and be disruptive in the backﬁeld. He has a chance to become a true off-ball linebacker in the NFL, but I think his best ﬁt is as a sub-package rusher on passing downs.

name: Jasheen Davis
strengths: ● Workable size and length for edge duties ● Never shuts it down and plays relentless in pursuit ● Leaving him alone on a tight end isn't advised for an offense ● Plants his heels, creates bend and holds up against double teams ● Plays well on his feet and ﬂashes a burst to the football mid-rush ● Violent chops/swipes to break down blockers ● Able to dip inside shoulder underneath the tackle ● Worked in a ghost move to take away his inside hand and dip around blocks ● You can see his passion for football on tape in the way he competes ● Consistent production each season as a starter
weaknesses: ● Inconsistent eyes ● Needs to wide vision in the run game to prevent getting washed by angle blocks ● Has length and strength to set the edge but too often gets stuck inside, losing contain responsibilities ● Doesn't always appear to rush with a plan ● Needs to improve aiming points as a leverage rusher to create movement ● Rarely see him drop into space on tape
summary: A four-year starter at Wake Forest, Davis was an edge defender in former defensive coordinator Brad Lambert's versatile fronts, lining up as a 4i-/seven-technique. The prize of the Demon Deacons' 2020 recruiting class, he led the team in sacks and tackles for loss each of the past three seasons and ﬁnished his career No. 2 in school history in tackles for loss (51) and No. 3 in sacks (25.5). Davis generates impressive force once he gets rolling downhill, ﬂashing the strong hands and contact balance to work off blockers. According to Wake Forest defensive line coach Dave Cohen, his energetic play style and motor compares to that of Kobie Turner as the best he has ever coached. Overall, Davis can get tied up too much in the run game, but his powerful hands/limbs and obsessive effort lead to production, especially as a pass rusher. He can offer an NFL defensive line immediate depth.

name: Seth Coleman
summary: Seth Coleman grew up on Florida's Atlantic coast and started playing football in ﬁrst grade, although basketball was his focus through childhood. He played both sports at Holy Trinity Episcopal Academy and received several basketball offers, but a big senior year on the football ﬁeld (101 tackles, 13 sacks) changed his outlook. A four-star recruit, he committed to Illinois (over Utah and others), initially lining up as a defensive end before moving to a stand-up edge role, from which he posted steady backﬁeld production the past four seasons. Coleman plays with effort and energy to aggressively attack the pocket, although his hands, feet and dip often feel disconnected when attempting different moves. Though his motor also translates to the run game, he has only average strength at the point of attack and can be late unwinding from blocks. Overall, Coleman doesn't bring much deception to his pass rush, but he offers length and burst to wrap the edge and affect the quarterback.

name: Garmon Randolph
summary: Garmon Randolph grew up down the road from Athens, Ga., with his parents (Joseph and Monja). His older brother (Joseph) played defensive line at The Citadel (2016-19). Randolph was known more at Jefferson High for what he could do at tight end (14 catches for 205 yards and ﬁve touchdowns as a senior), but he also played defensive end (34 tackles, one sack and one interception, which he returned for a touchdown). A three-star recruit, he committed to Baylor and then-coach Matt Rhule over offers from Alabama, Michigan and others. Randolph moved to defense full time and played a variety of front-seven roles over the past six years for the Bears, primarily as a stand-up edge rusher. He has an explosive ﬁrst step as a rusher and smooth movement skills when dropping into space. A taller player, he gets upright when setting the edge, but his length and hand strength help him win battles. His motor also jumps out, although his hard-charging style leads to too many missed tackles. Overall, Randolph is still learning how to fully weaponize his size and athleticism, but it feels like there is untapped talent ready to be developed.

name: Elijah Alston
summary: Elijah "Eli" Alston grew up in the Chesapeake, Va., area and started playing football at age 5. He was a four-year letterman as a defensive end at Oscar Smith High, helping the team to three straight state title games. A three-star recruit, he received his ﬁrst offer from James Madison but ultimately chose Marshall, because his mother (La Juan Stepney) encouraged him to leave the state to experience something new. He became a starter at Marshall, then entered the transfer portal after the 2023 season and committed to Miami over Texas A&M and others (Miami's defensive coordinator in 2024 was Lance Guidry, Marshall's defensive coordinator in 2021-22). Playing mostly as a Jack edge rusher, Alston was asked to rush, drop and ﬂatten to make plays down the line. He has enough strength in his frame to set an edge and constrict run lanes. I like his effort on defense and special teams, although I don't think he has the speed for special teams coverages in the NFL. Overall, Alston is only an average athlete, but he plays with energy to make plays against both pass and run, which can earn him a practice squad spot.

name: Mason Graham
strengths: ● Thick, square build with naturally low pads to win the leverage battle ● Strong at the point of attack with above-average instincts against the run ● Explosive by nature to fire off the ball and drive opponents into the lap of the quarterback ● Quick feet and hands as a pass rusher to cross the face of blockers, win half-man and knife into the backfield ● Agile athleticism is evident on stunts and loops ● Twitchy in his upper half for strong push-pulls and understands how to dismantle balance of blockers ● Moves well laterally with relentless effort to consistently make plays away from starting point ● Missed tackles were hard to find on his 2024 film ● Blocked field goal on against Washington in 2024 THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 325 ● Calls out blocking schemes pre-snap — football IQ jumped each season ● Low-key personality off the ﬁeld but violent competitor on it ● Played ﬁve different sports in high school, which helped unlock his physical abilities
weaknesses: ● Average body type and lacks desired length ● Doesn't always create clear separation after initial punch ● NFL scouts say there is some sloppy weight on his frame ● Anchor breaks down against double teams and redirect blocks ● Inconsistent sifting through traffic ● Needs to add more variety to pass-rush attack ● Broke left thumb as a junior (Sept. 2023) and required surgery, but he only missed two weeks and returned with a club on his left hand
summary: A two-year starter at Michigan, Graham was a three-technique defensive tackle in defensive coordinator Wink Martindale's four-man front (76.6 percent of his career snaps came over the B-gap). Although his backﬁeld production doesn't jump off the stat sheet, Graham was arguably the most valuable defensive player on the Wolverines' 2023 national championship team and played even better (with lesser talent around him) in 2024. Graham naturally plays from a low position to consistently win leverage through contact — he credits his athletic twitch and understanding of angles to his championship-level wrestling background. He needs to develop his efficiency versus double teams, but he violently sheds single blocks and plays the piano up and down the line with his outstanding chase effort. Overall, Graham is a leverage monster and skillfully destroys blocks with his strength, quickness, motor and play recognition to make an impact versus both pass and run. He projects as a versatile interior presence with the ﬂoor of an NFL starter.

name: Derrick Harmon
strengths: ● Athletic big man with desired size, length and quickness ● Big, heavy guards struggle to match his lateral agility ● Upper-body strength and physical swipe/rip moves give him access to gaps ● Varies rush moves and is always looking to mix in new tactics ● Finds wrists/arms of blockers and throws them away ● Closes in a ﬂash once he has a lane to the ball carrier ● Shoots downhill to win front-side angles and blow up ball carrier at the line of scrimmage ● Can hold his ground in the run game, against either single or double blocks ● Dogged effort is his calling card when chasing ● Durable; didn't miss a game over his ﬁnal three college seasons
weaknesses: ● Good-looking frame but has some sloppy weight on his body ● Below-average ﬁnisher and must become a better tackler in backﬁeld ● Throws the kitchen sink at blockers and is still learning how to efficiently streamline his attack ● Relies more on quickness than block reads when attacking the run ● More consistent pad level will improve his anchor ● Too many undisciplined penalties on his 2024 tape (roughing the passer, unnecessary roughness, hands to the face) ● Arrived at Michigan State as a 350-pound freshman — conditioning will be key
summary: A one-year starter at Oregon, Harmon lined up primarily over the B-gap in defensive coordinator Tosh Lupoi's multiple fronts. He ﬂashed promise at Michigan State before transferring to Eugene and producing his breakout season in 2024, when he led all FBS interior defensive linemen with 55 pressures (12 more than the next-closest DT). A player who can win in different ways, Harmon forces blockers to attack air with his lateral explosiveness or uses strong, crafty hands to swat away the reach of blockers as he bursts through gaps to close on the ball carrier. Though he led FBS interior linemen in pressures, he also led the position in missed tackles (12) — even the smallest improvements in his backﬁeld ﬁnishing ability would have resulted in double-digit sacks. Overall, Harmon is a highly active and disruptive big man who consistently ﬁnds ways to gain freedom from blocks as a penetrating pass rusher and run stuffer. He projects as a scheme-diverse NFL starter, anywhere from one- to ﬁve-tech.

name: Kenneth Grant
strengths: ● Wide-bodied lineman with thickness throughout and unique athleticism ("Freaks List" alum) ● Moves with big-man balance and ﬂexible hips to swim through gaps ● Uses lateral range to work up and down the line ● Tough to move him off his spot ● Plenty of natural power behind his active, physical hands ● Locks out with his arms to control blocks and muck up things inside ● Rare speed and hustle for his size to close the gap when chasing ball carrier ● Smoothly calms his feet on the move to gobble up ball carriers and ﬁnish tackles ● Has a knack for getting his big mitts up (10 combined pass breakups past two seasons) ● Not overly vocal, but the coaches say he took on more of a leadership role in 2024
weaknesses: ● Slow-burn pass rusher with an undeveloped plan if his ﬁrst move is ineffective ● Elevated pad level will leave him uprooted and neutralized post-snap ● Delivers initial pop but struggles to create a consistent pocket push ● Late to read blocking scheme or ball carrier at times ● His weight will climb north of 350 pounds in the offseason, and his conditioning needs monitored ● Didn't miss a game because of injury in Ann Arbor but battled through right foot tendinitis as a high school senior ● Tackle production (on either side of the line of scrimmage) doesn't jump out
summary: A two-year starter at Michigan, Grant was an interchangeable defensive tackle in defensive coordinator Wink Martindale's four-man front, lining up as both a three-technique and nose tackle. He went viral during the 2023 season when he chased down Penn State running back Kaytron Allen in the open ﬁeld, and he was a steady presence on the Wolverines' defensive line the past two seasons. A dominant run presence, Grant is a powerful boulder who can execute two-gap techniques or stack single blocks and work down the line with quickness. He looks to ﬁre off the ball, although his tall pads will negate his leverage and lower-body strength, diminishing his bull rush and limiting the ways in which he can impact the quarterback. Overall, Grant plays big in a big man's game, but he also has the athletic traits and effort to grow into more than just a stout run stopper. He projects as an early-down NFL starter with three-down upside.

name: Walter Nolen
strengths: ● Explosive ﬁrst step with equally explosive hands ● Has initial movements to cross face, shoot gaps and live in gaps ● Weaponizes length to stab and ﬂashes a twitchy slap/arm-over move ● Relies on get-off quickness as his source of power to create push at contact ● Rangy athlete for his size, with the secondary quickness to ﬁnish behind the line of scrimmage ● Quick to ﬁnd his balance to react to the ball carrier and get him on the ground ● Strong tackler in close quarters (rarely missed tackles) ● Able to plant his post leg and hold his own against doubles ● Plays hard, and his effort doesn't see major dips snap to snap ● Production improved each season — ﬁnished top three among FBS interior defensive linemen in tackles for loss in 2024
weaknesses: ● Can do a better job staying square when moving laterally down the line ● Reacts ﬁrst and reads second, leaving him out of position at times THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 329 ● Rush plan is based more on activity than cohesion ● Improving his lock-out will help keep his eyes elevated to ﬁnd the football ● Personal foul on the 2024 Arkansas tape for extracurricular efforts ● Disappears on some tapes; averaged only 2.7 pressures per game in 2024 ● Attended six different programs over the last seven years, so interview process will be crucial to his ﬁnal grade
summary: A one-year starter at Ole Miss, Nolen played three-technique tackle in defensive coordinator Pete Golding's 4-2-5 base scheme, occasionally lining up over or outside the tackle. A consensus top-ﬁve recruit out of high school, he played two mediocre seasons at Texas A&M before transferring to Oxford, where he had his best season in 2024, joining Patrick Willis as the only consensus All-Americans from the front seven in school history. With his length and surge off the ball, Nolen creates immediate force and can be a play-wrecker with how quickly he penetrates gaps (the type of leverage that creates holding calls). He doesn't rely on just quickness to win, but there are inefficiencies in his attack, especially when he is late to read the play. Overall, Nolen has areas of his game that require maturing, but he ﬂashes big-time disruption in his initial burst and fast, physical hands to regularly affect the backﬁeld action. He will be attractive for NFL teams looking for an active gap-shooter with high-end upside.

name: Tyleik Williams
strengths: ● Owns a thick frame with large hands ● Quickly breaks down blocks in the run game with hip explosion and extension at contact ● Maintains gap integrity and uses natural leverage to stay balanced through congestion ● Upﬁeld burst once he defeats the hands of blockers ● Tough guy to slow down once he gets his momentum downhill through gaps THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 330 ● Terriﬁc block awareness and has a feel for splitting double teams ● Creates more penalties than he commits ● Sniffs out screens and understands where the offense wants to attack ● Always in pursuit mode — frequently makes tackles away from his square ● Weighed more than 360 pounds when he enrolled and worked hard to keep a steady weight
weaknesses: ● Below-average length and can be out-levered if he doesn't win off the snap ● Doesn't consistently collapse the pocket as a pass rusher ● Not known for his ability to counter and has some stiffness attempting to redirect ● Needs to mature his pass-rush plan beyond his initial attack ● Strong backs can run through his ﬁngertip tackles (see 2024 Penn State tape) ● Missed three games as senior with lower-body injury (Sept. 2024) and ankle issue (Nov. 2024); battled shoulder, elbow and knee injuries throughout 2022 season
summary: A two-year starter at Ohio State, Williams played the three-technique position in former defensive coordinator Jim Knowles' four-man front. His production won't jump off the page — he ﬁnished 10th in tackles (46) and sixth in sacks (2.5) for the Buckeyes' national title-winning squad in 2024. But his impact as a dominant run defender is much clearer on the tape. With his initial quickness, Williams can cross the face of blockers or create knockback with his ability to stack, ﬁnd the football and detach. Aside from his physical capabilities, he has outstanding awareness to identify pre-snap clues and anticipate play design. Overall, Williams needs further development as a pass rusher, but he is one of the best run-defending linemen in the draft class because of his recognition skills and disciplined execution at deconstructing blocks. He has the type of skill set that will be appreciated by NFL coaches.

name: Shemar Turner
strengths: ● Explosive in his lower half and through his hips ● Added 30 pounds before 2024 season but didn't sacriﬁce initial quickness to squeeze gaps ● Flashes quick-swim and violent club-rip moves to power through shoulders ● Effective on stunts and games that get him free ● Hands are active and strong to snatch/pull blockers ● Able to lock out, sumo sit and track football in the backﬁeld ● Grew up idolizing Ray Lewis and plays with similar on-ﬁeld violence ● Willing to throw the ﬁrst punch (both literally and ﬁguratively) ● NFL scouts describe him as a "foxhole-type" and "outstanding teammate" ● Consistently plays through pain, including a stress fracture during the 2024 season
weaknesses: ● Adrenaline is overﬂowing and compete skills border on reckless ● Flagged seven times for personal foul penalties over past two seasons (ﬁve in 2024, two in 2023) ● Ejected from a game (Nov. 2023) after throwing multiple punches at an Ole Miss blocker, including an uppercut to the groin (Stewart called his actions unacceptable and tweeted an apology for "embarrassing myself, my family and my team") ● Needs to improve aiming points for more efficient stack and shed ● Inconsistent gap integrity and can be pushed away from run lane ● Lackluster secondary moves as a pass rusher ● Sloppy tendencies as tackler (double-digit misses on his 2024 tape) ● Off-ﬁeld decision-making will be scrutinized after he was arrested and charged with reckless driving during his junior season (Sept. 2023); he faced "internal discipline" and didn't miss any playing time. ● Stress fracture during 2024 fall camp (that required a rod be inserted) and played through the injury, but it didn't heal properly and he missed a portion of the draft process; played through a torn labrum over the second half of the 2023 season and underwent offseason surgery; underwent surgery following the 2023 season for a shin injury (June 2024)
summary: A three-year starter at Texas A&M, Turner played a three-technique role as a senior in head coach Mike Elko's four-man front, logging snaps everywhere from zero- to seven-technique. After playing primarily on the edge as an underclassman, he added weight for the transition inside in 2024 and made his presence known on every tape studied, despite playing through a stress fracture. With his active motor and body quickness, Turner ﬁnds ways to pierce gaps and affect the backﬁeld action. He has a strong, explosive grip to snatch and displace blockers in the run game, although he can be a liability at times when he abandons his gap or fails to break down and ﬁnish. Much will be made of his overzealous tendencies, which draw attention from officials, but as one scout described him: "He's the type you want on your side." Overall, Turner needs to introduce more discipline to his play style, but he prides himself on being the aggressor and relies on his initial twitch, ﬁerce hands and combative mentality to be a factor. He projects best as a penetrating one-gap tackle.

name: Darius Alexander
strengths: ● Owns an NFL-ready frame, with long arms and big hands ● Fluid big man with outstanding body control for his size to slip through gaps ● Works well laterally to make plays up and down the line ● Shows basic understanding of how to lock out and leverage blocks, both as a rusher and run defender ● Rudely introduces himself to blockers with ﬁrm punches to create control ● Uses forceful tugs and rips to cross the faces of blockers ● Saw snaps on the edge, where he could tilt the ﬁeld and create push with an extended runway ● Sniffs out screens and plays alert as a drop player (see his interception in 2024 bowl game) ● Dominated against stiffer competition during Senior Bowl practices
weaknesses: ● Finds himself too upright with only average contact strength to battle through blocks ● Needs to develop instincts to feel blocking pressure and anticipate scheme ● Rangy tackler, but he'll leave some production on the ﬁeld when he plays too hot ● Fights through traffic, but his rush plan often lacks cohesiveness ● Didn't dominate in college to the level his talent suggests he should have ● Single-digit career sacks over 59 games in college ● Will be 25 as a rookie
summary: A two-year starter at Toledo, Alexander played primarily the three-technique position in defensive coordinator Vince Kehres' hybrid front. The Rockets' coaches initially played him at offensive tackle his ﬁrst year in the program before moving him to the defensive line. His development was more gradual than immediate in college, but he ﬂashed high-end ability over his ﬁnal two seasons (led the team in pressures created in 2023 and 2024) and didn't disappoint under the microscope at Senior Bowl practices. Alexander is rangy defending the run, with the body ﬂuidity and length to displace blocks. He has shown an improved ability to feel the rhythm of blocks to work off contact but needs to streamline his pass rush with more consistent leverage and sequencing. Overall, Alexander isn't yet the full sum of his impressive parts, but his blend of power, length and athletic body control give him the makings of a three-down, scheme-versatile NFL starter. He projects best in an attacking role, where he'd be able to maximize his disruptive traits. His peak plays are reminiscent of Leonard Williams.

name: Alfred Collins
strengths: ● Broad-framed with exceptional height-weight-length combination ● Creates movement with natural power behind swats/strikes ● Uses wide base, body control and long arms to leverage blockers off balance ● Can get blockers moving one way before cutting back toward the pocket ● Agile-footed for his size, with the tools to play multiple gaps and ﬂatten down the line ● Elite tackle-to-missed tackle ratio in 2024 (55:2) ● Matured play recognition helps him cover more ground than expected (see forced fumble on 2024 Arkansas tape) ● Blocked a ﬁeld goal as senior; six batted passes at line in 2024 tied for No. 2 in FBS ● Played more snaps in 2024 but effort level didn't decline ● Proven durability — played in 64 of 65 games over ﬁve years in Austin
weaknesses: ● Comes off ball tall and will struggle to get underneath blocks ● Leggy; high center disrupts his ability to quickly change directions ● Plays hard but too much wasted movement in his hands trying to wrestle free ● Not consistently explosive separating from blocks, especially later in games ● When given chances to rush the passer, his moves lacked efficiency with inconsistent counters THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 334 ● Missed part of the draft process because of a left calf strain ● Played only one season as a full-time star
summary: A one-year starter at Texas, Collins played nose tackle in defensive coordinator Pete Kwiatkowski's front, although he saw most of his 2024 snaps over the B-gap (299, compared to 145 over the A-gap and 129 over the tackle). Highly recruited out of the Austin area, he was given an "underachiever" label by some while playing behind T'Vondre Sweat and Byron Murphy III in 2023, but he played his best ball in 2024 with starting-level snaps. A coordinated big man, Collins plays with natural power and does a great job as a two-gapper, stacking, peeking and grounding ball carriers between the tackles. His hands are more heavy than disciplined, and he struggles to root himself versus doubles because of his tall pads. Overall, Collins is still learning how to maximize his size and talent, but he took a sizable jump this past season and shows the physical traits to be a disruptive force, especially against the run. He will provide immediate depth as a rookie, and his snap count should increase with experience.

name: T.J. Sanders
strengths: ● Tall, athletic frame with long arms and range ● Light on his feet and moves well laterally to access different gaps ● Fluid off blocks to close on the football ● Flashes violence in his hands to shed and make stops at the line ● Active on loops and will get skinny on stunts/twists THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 335 ● Can push the pocket when he creates downhill momentum ● More physical at the point of attack than expected for his size ● Loses slowly versus double teams and two-gaps with control when needed ● Covers ground from the backside with a consistent motor ● NFL scout: "The coaches say he really matured and went from being late to meetings when he ﬁrst got there to becoming a guy who sets the example of how to carry himself as an upperclassman."
weaknesses: ● Lacks desired mass to combat NFL power in trenches ● Savvy blockers will use his aggressiveness against him ● Inconsistent resisting pressure on angle/down blocks and can be caught out of position ● Caught leaning on blocks ● Can do a better job countering once pads become elevated and ﬁrst move is halted ● Has some rough stretches as tackler (see 2024 Vanderbilt tape) ● Average production reﬂects his average awareness
summary: A two-year starter at South Carolina, Sanders was a versatile defensive tackle in defensive coordinator Clayton White's four-man front, aligning up and down the line of scrimmage. A late bloomer (Sanders didn't focus on football until his junior year in high school), his impact steadily improved each of his four seasons as part of a deep, talented Gamecocks defensive line (averaged just 36 defensive snaps in 2024). With his initial burst, Sanders can maneuver through gaps with abrupt hands/feet or change the line of scrimmage by quickly getting into a blocker's chest. He is surprisingly stout at the point of attack and ﬂashes power and hand use to stack and shed against the run. Overall, Sanders is a long, twitchy big man and has the tools to make consistent plays in the backﬁeld with continued technical and awareness improvements. His promising skill set will ﬁt both even and odd fronts.

name: Joshua Farmer
strengths: ● Broad, thick build with big hands and long arms (NFL scout: "He was in the best shape of his life when the season kicked off this year.") ● Explosive mover to attack gaps like a bull in a china shop ● Quick, ﬁerce hands to stab/swipe and work off contact (doesn't like to wear gloves) ● Uses a variety of club moves to blow through shoulders of blockers ● Rushes with joint bend to get underneath blocks and unlock leverage ● Keeps tabs on the ball with backﬁeld vision ● Played senior year of high school at 255 pounds and pushed himself in the weight room ● Team captain in 2024 — his alpha attitude started to show
weaknesses: ● Inconsistent snap anticipation (two offsides ﬂags on 2024 Duke tape) ● Linear pass-rush approach and inconsistent adjusting path ● Hands are forceful but often mistimed ● Needs to better transition to swim/arm-over techniques once initial rush is stalled ● Streaky anchor, mostly because of issues with pad level ● Needs to do better job as a read player to feel screens ● College production doesn't grab the eye ● Played through thumb injury for most of 2023 season and underwent surgery (Dec. 2023), which sidelined him for bowl game and part of the offseason training
summary: A two-year starter at Florida State, Farmer lined up as a 2i-/three-technique in former defensive coordinator Adam Fuller's four-man front. He showed gradual improvements over his four seasons in Tallahassee, as he embraced coaching and matured his body, ﬁnishing second on the team in pressures (26). Farmer is a burly, power-packed lineman who can deliver pop at contact and get himself free with his active hands and short-area quickness. He can muddy things up in the run game, although his base strength shows cracks when he loses leverage, and his block recognition must continue to develop. Overall, Farmer goes through too many quiet stretches on ﬁlm, but he is a force creator with his natural power as a two-gapper and promising pass-rush tools. He should step into a rotation as a rookie and has the potential of a full-time starter.

name: Ty Hamilton
strengths: ● Compact frame and comfortably carries added weight ● Large, physical hands and continues to pound on the door ● Creates initial knockback at the point of attack to disrupt run angles ● Moves well laterally with coordinated feet to quickly catch his balance ● Strong backﬁeld vision to stay gap sound and play the cutback ● Snaps per game almost doubled in 2024, but his motor stayed cranked ● Described as "quiet but cold-blooded" by the coaches (Ryan Day: "He's the ultimate team player. Doesn't say a whole lot, but goes to work every day.") ● Reliable — played in all 55 games over past four seasons
weaknesses: ● Average length and likely at max playing weight ● Has some lower-body stiffness, which hinders his quick redirect skills ● Plays with decent anchor but can be moved by double teams ● Initial quickness is better than his gap-penetrating quickness ● Plays high as a pass rusher, with a limited arsenal of pass-rush moves ● Able to collapse the pocket, but it takes him time to get there
summary: A two-year starter at Ohio State, Hamilton played out of position as the nose tackle in former defensive coordinator Jim Knowles' four-man front. A late bloomer on the football ﬁeld, like his older brother, he added 30 pounds for a move from defensive end to tackle and evolved into a valuable part of the Buckeyes' national title-winning team in 2024. With his initial quickness and block awareness, Hamilton initiates leveraged contact to stack blocks, create push and shed versus the run. Though he has one-gap traits, he plays with two-gap technique and was asked to do a lot of dirty work in college to make life easier for the linebackers. Overall, Hamilton needs pass-rush development, but he is quick, forceful and urgent to create disruption within the structure of the defense. His coachable attitude and position versatility raise his NFL ﬂoor as a role player and potential starter.

weaknesses: ● More average than above-average as an athlete ● Upright with tightness through his hips and ankles ● Provides initial pop, but his feet slow at contact and blockers are able to settle down against his power ● Hands are active but not consistently well-timed for easy transitions ● Inconsistent balance — on the ground more than you'd like ● Arrives too hot and leaves too much tackle production on the ﬁeld ● Will turn 24 shortly after draft weekend
summary: A ﬁve-year starter at Nebraska, Robinson was an interchangeable defensive lineman in former defensive coordinator Tony White's 3-3-5 scheme, lining up as the nose, 3-/4i-technique and wide of the tackle. He returned for his sixth year and helped Nebraska achieve its ﬁrst winning record in almost a decade, posting personal bests across the board with 42 pressures, 12.5 tackles for loss and seven sacks. When he stays low with forward lean off the snap, Robinson can slant and shoot through gaps like a locomotive off the tracks, although his attack is much more methodical if he doesn't win quickly and has to play through contact. He has natural football instincts with play-recognition skills that show against the pass and the run. Overall, Robinson might lack star potential, but rugged competitors with his size, toughness and ability never go out of style in the NFL. He projects as a rotational defender who ﬁts both even (one-technique) and odd (4i-/ﬁve-technique) fronts.

summary: A three-year starter at UCLA, Toia was the zero-/one-technique in defensive coordinator Ikaika Malloe's 3-3-5 base scheme. His production on paper doesn't jump out, but the tape shows a player willing to chew up blocks in the middle, freeing linebackers and ends to make plays. When he plays with consistent leverage, Toia is able to put down roots and shut down inside run lanes. However, he must continue to develop his instincts to create tackle opportunities, instead of just taking up room. Overall, Toia might not have the length or awareness to be a full-time two-gapper in the NFL, but he has a powerful base and physical hands to neutralize the point of attack. He projects as a scheme-versatile nose tackle.

summary: A two-year starter at Florida, Jackson was the nose tackle in co-defensive coordinator Austin Armstrong's scheme, playing primarily on early downs (averaged 28.8 defensive snaps per game over his two seasons in Gainesville). After his full ride to LSU fell through, he earned Memphis' attention before ﬁnally making it to the SEC as a dominant run defender with the Gators. A massive human (you don't need to know his jersey number to spot him on tape), Jackson occupies space and is able to eat up double teams to keep linebackers clean behind him. He ﬂashes power to big-boy blockers but doesn't consistently sustain and collapse the pocket, which limits his role on sub-package downs. Overall, Jackson has a shallow toolbox as a pass rusher, but he is a solid athlete for his size and a tough player to displace as a two-gapping run stuffer. Regardless of scheme, he offers value as an early-down NFL nose who can anchor and eat up blocks.

Since he played limited snaps on the Vols' heavy-rotation defensive line (20th on the team in defensive snaps in 2024), his production volume doesn't jump out, but he led all FBS interior defensive linemen in 2024 in pass rush win rate (12.6 percent) and win percentage (18.9 percent). Often the ﬁrst defender to cross the line of scrimmage, Norman-Lott is a twitched-up big man with a diverse skill set to win one-on-one matchups with quickness, power or leverage. He uses sound hand/move fundamentals but leaves a lot of tackle production on the ﬁeld and needs to play with better control. Overall, Norman-Lott is an explosive disruptor and offers high upside for a coaching staff that can harness his energy, THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 343 although he will need to improve his undisciplined tendencies, especially in the run game. There is no doubt about his NFL talent, but his ability to handle more of a full-time role is a tricky projection.

summary: A two-year starter at Maryland, Phillips was an interchangeable defensive tackle in defensive coordinator Brian Williams' hybrid fronts, lining up everywhere from head-up nose to ﬁve-technique (mostly in a frog stance). After one season in Knoxville, he transferred to Maryland and showed noticeable promise, despite remarkably low production (2.5 tackles for loss and zero sacks over 23 starts). A toolsy prospect, Phillips jumps off the ﬁlm with his light feet, explosive movements and heavy hands. Though it is encouraging that he is one of the youngest players in the draft class, his inexperience jumps off the ﬁlm — he's often neutralized and off balance, especially when he is late off the ball. Overall, Phillips is a dancing bear with big-man twitch and commanding power, but his immense talent needs to be unlocked by more mature timing and technique. Although he will need time, he has the traits and work ethic to become a rotational nose with the upside of an NFL starter.

summary: A one-year starter at Virginia Tech, Peebles manned the three-technique tackle in head coach Brent Pry's four-man front, also seeing snaps at 4i-/ﬁve-technique. After leading Duke in tackles for loss and sacks in 2023, he fell short of that production with the Hokies in 2024 (although, his 37 pressures ranked third among all FBS interior defensive lineman). With his ﬁrst-step quickness and non-stop energy, Peebles ﬂashes as a pass rusher and competes with the urgency to affect the backﬁeld action. He plays with balance at contact but lacks the mass, length and anchor that teams generally desire, especially in the run game. Overall, Peebles has an unconventional body type, which raises obvious concerns about his NFL transition, but he is a spirited pass rusher with serious juice and a diverse set of tactics to be disruptive. He projects as a rotational backup as a penetrating one-gapper who can carve out a role as a sub-down rusher. GRADE: 3rd-4th round

strengths: ● Played three-technique at Houston and nose tackle at Oregon — offers experience at both ● Carries weight smoothly for a thick 332-pounder ● Flashes short-area quickness to attack edges and play in gaps ● Built low and wins with leverage to play underneath blocks ● Can deliver blows and put blockers on their heels ● Strong through his core and hips to maintain positioning ● Steady activity level, with ball-searching eyes ● Blocked a pair of ﬁeld goals in two seasons at Houston ● Played entire 2023 season with a hard cast after breaking his left hand in the opener ● Started every game in 2024 and was a consistent presence

summary: A one-year starter at Oregon, Caldwell was the nose tackle (zero-/2i-technique) in defensive coordinator Tosh Lupoi's multiple fronts. After temporarily stepping away from football in 2020, he walked on at the junior college level and worked his way to Houston, where he became a disruptive three-technique (despite playing the entire 2023 season with a hard cast after breaking his hand in the opener). After transferring to Oregon, he showed his willingness to do whatever was asked by adding weight and playing more of a plugger role (2.1 tackles per game in 2024). Caldwell is an interesting study, because he has the look of a squatty nose but the quickness and activity level of a one-gapper with the potential to impact the backﬁeld (Caldwell: "I see myself as a pure three-tech, but I can do both."). He can explode into blockers to create pop, although I worry about NFL centers reaching/sealing him — he needs to be more consistent with his hands for quicker sheds, if he hopes to turn his potential into more production. Overall, the tape runs hot and cold for Caldwell, and he plays with a confused identity. However, he has an interesting collection of traits and put a little bit of everything on tape, which will make him appealing to different schemes. I like him best as a rotational one-technique who can stay on the ﬁeld on passing downs.

summary: A three-year starter at Kentucky, Walker was an interchangeable defensive lineman in defensive coordinator Brad White's scheme (45.7 percent of his 2024 snaps came as a three-technique DT, 26.3 percent as a one-technique/nose, 25 percent head-up on or outside of the offensive tackle). After earning preliminary ﬁrst-round grades from scouts as a sophomore, his junior season wasn't nearly as dominant or consistent (pressures created dropped from 51 in 2023 to 21 in 2024), partly because of his back injury. A passionate basketball player through high school, Walker certainly beneﬁts from the "planet theory" — there are only so many humans walking the earth who have his combination of size, strength and sweet feet. Though he doesn't play stiff, there are sloppy elements of his game that must improve to streamline his ability to stack, shed and ﬁnish. Overall, Walker is a unique athlete with impressive balance and movement skills for a 330-plus-pounder, but his technique and pad level must catch up with his physical talent for the ﬂashes to become consistent. If he adapts to pro coaching, he has the skill set to become an NFL starter.
