name: Jason Marshall Jr.
strengths: ● Plays with a ton of conﬁdence in man-to-man, his preferred coverage ● Good-looking athlete who can match up with big and small pass catchers ● Teases explosiveness and balance in movements ● Efficiently sorts through stacks and combination routes ● Locates and makes plays on the ball from trail coverage ● Muddies catch points with his physical nature (led team in passes defended in 2022 and 2023) ● Plays through contact well and gets physical early in rep ● Started almost immediately as freshman and was battle-tested in the SEC
weaknesses: ● His last interception came the weekend before Thanksgiving 2022 ● Looks like a technician on some plays, then doesn't trust his foundation the next play ● Average trigger burst from off coverage ● Eyes pay rent in the backﬁeld, and play fakes create wasted reaction steps ● Crossers can gain a step on him too easily ● Willing in run support, but reckless tendencies need to be ﬁxed to help avoid misses ● Needs to expand his special teams resume at next level ● Suffered torn labrum as senior (Oct. 2024), which required season-ending surgery
summary: A four-year starter at Florida, Marshall was an outside cornerback in former defensive coordinator Austin Armstrong's multiple coverage scheme. A former ﬁve-star recruit, he was an immediate contributor in Gainesville and ﬂashed his talent early, although he struggled to take the next step in his development (seven receiving touchdowns allowed, zero interceptions the past two seasons). Marshall displays the feet to press and smoothly transition with route breaks, although he has trouble making up ground once he loses a step in coverage. He struggles to anticipate from depth and stay ahead of plays. He also needs to be more aggressive in his approach, including as a run defender. Overall, Marshall has the size and athletic ability to tighten throwing windows in man coverage, but inconsistent reads and reactions are too common on his tape. If NFL teams are convinced he is coachable, he is a worthy draft-and-develop candidate.

name: Alijah Huzzie
strengths: ● Moves with balance and body control ● On-ball production a consistent theme each season ● Catches ball with ease (16 career interceptions) ● Anticipates catch windows in tight coverage to accurately time swipes ● Widescreen vision to get eyes on both receiver and quarterback ● Honed patience and ﬁnishing skills as tackler in 2024 ● Two punt return touchdowns while at North Carolina; averaged 13.9 yards per return in his career (19 attempts for 265 yards) ● Tough-minded and "works at his craft," according to an NFL scout ● Played a lot of football (54 career starts) with experience both inside and outside

He started out at East Tennessee State before transferring to Chapel Hill the past two seasons. He accumulated an eye-popping 60 passes defended and 16 interceptions over the past ﬁve years. Huzzie has terriﬁc balance and footwork in coverage and was one of the winners during East-West Shrine Bowl practices, because of his efficient movements in drills. He ﬂashes playmaking ability, while offering punt return value and the mental makeup for sub packages. name: Jaylin Smith
strengths: ● Very good lateral quickness to match receivers in press ● Conﬁdent speed and redirect skills to hold up on an island ● Good look-and-lean technique and presses receivers to the sideline ● Trusts route anticipation to put him in position to make plays on the ball ● Gets hands inside frame of receivers to hitch a ride in trail ● Plays with dog mentality as a run defender and in coverage ● Good tempo to weave around pulling blocks and dismantle screens ● Stood out on punt coverages as a gunner and jammer ● Versatile experience across the secondary at corner, safety and nickel
weaknesses: ● Averaged-framed; lacks ideal mass and growth potential ● Better feistiness than play strength ● Only average burst when attempting to close out throws ● Inconsistent reacting to throws with his back to the ball THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 458 ● Below-average ball production for a player with his experience ● Doesn't have length to compensate for poor technique in run support ● Leaves his feet prematurely, resulting in ankle-biting tackle attempts ● Staying healthy has been an issue: missed last two games as freshman after suffering concussion (Nov. 2021); missed ﬁnal three games of 2022 season because of injury; missed one game as junior (Nov. 2023) and two more as senior (Sept. 2024) because of injuries
summary: A three-year starter at USC, Smith moved from the nickel to outside cornerback in defensive coordinator D'Anton Lynn's man/zone scheme. Compared to his 2023 tape, he made key improvements as a senior in both coverage and run support — he did not allow a touchdown catch in 2024 and set a career high with two interceptions. Although he is more quick than explosive, Smith has smooth movements in space to transition or ride the hip pocket with different types of route runners. He gets nose to nose with receivers in press and overlaps well from zone looks, but his ball instincts were lacking on tape (just eight passes defended over 32 career starts). He will need to prove he can stay healthy to stick on a roster.

name: BJ Adams
strengths: ● Above-average height and length to match up with NFL size ● Covers a lot of air space to swipe away throws ● Plays physical brand of football with punchy jam ● Efficient opening his hips from press to ride routes ● Flashes an extra gear late when closing on catch point ● Improved ability to throttle down and sting as tackler ● Played on kick and punt coverages all four seasons (371 career special teams snaps) THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 459

summary: A one-year starter at UCF, Adams was an outside cornerback in former defensive coordinator Addison Williams' multiple coverage scheme (Cover 2, Cover 3 and press man). He worked his way into the starting rotation as a true freshman and played in 48 games over the past four years, although he never had more than four passes defended in any of those seasons. Adams puts his length to good use when he redirects receivers at the line and makes them uncomfortable throughout the route. He can take away passing windows with his size, but his tape doesn't show natural ball instincts, and he must become more disciplined in his process. Overall, Adams is long-limbed with enough athleticism to match routes from press, but he plays wild and upright in his movements, and his freelancing technique leads to spacing issues that NFL receivers will exploit. He is a developmental option for man-heavy teams.

name: Mello Dotson
strengths: ● Checks height box with solid arm length for the position ● Plays with natural feel for coverage and stays in phase with body control ● Uses length to take away passing lanes (35 passes defended over past three seasons) ● Makes quarterbacks pay for poor decisions THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 460 ● Has some juice after interception — set Kansas record with four career pick sixes ● Very reserved and quiet off ﬁeld (NFL scout: "He's basically the opposite personality of Cobee (Bryant).") ● Finished career with 38 consecutive starts
weaknesses: ● Middling long speed by NFL standards ● Can get beat over the top and is forced to protect himself against verticals ● Plays tall, which hinders quick transitions ● Very slender with marginal ﬁnishing strength, which shows in his tackling ● Lacks urgency getting off blocks ● Outside-only cornerback with almost no slot experience ● Very little special teams experience, outside of ﬁeld goal coverages
summary: A four-year starter at Kansas, Dotson was an outside cornerback in defensive coordinator Brian Borland's multiple coverage scheme. With Cobee Bryant, he formed one of the best cornerback duos in college football the past few seasons and ﬁnished his career with 12 interceptions, fourth most in school history. Dotson is a long, instinctive cornerback with the quiet conﬁdence to sniff out routes. Although he can get a little tight at the top of routes, he trusts his eyes to lead him to the football and has the ball skills to do something about it (231 career interception return yards). Overall, Dotson lacks elite foot agility and long speed for man coverage, but he shows a good feel for what the offense is trying to do and reacts accordingly. He will be a potential target late in the draft for a zone-heavy team.

name: Jabbar Muhammad
strengths: ● Tremendous ball instincts, putting himself in position to make plays ● Above-average on-ball production, with double-digit passes defended each of the past three seasons ● Always on high alert to make plays outside of his area ● Silky smooth hips for smooth transitions ● Leverages ﬁeld/sideline and maintains proper positioning ● Takes calculated chances, while also being fearless to jump routes ● Made clear improvements as tackler in 2024, showing better throttle and control as a ﬁnisher ● Never gets bored out there — all of his former coaches praise his competitive mentality
weaknesses: ● Thin-framed with poor height and arm length ● Non-explosive mover and doesn't have the long speed to make up ground ● Leaves some interceptions on the ﬁeld because of his lack of ideal size ● Larger receivers have little trouble overwhelming him at the catch point ● Caught leaning into receivers and ﬁnds himself off balance ● Ball carriers will carry him for extra yardage ● Inconsistent run defender, and his strength doesn't consistently match his intentions ● Older prospect — will turn 24 as an NFL rookie
summary: A one-year starter at Oregon, Muhammad was primarily an outside cornerback in defensive coordinator Tosh Lupoi's balanced coverage scheme. After starting his college career at Oklahoma State, he became a gun for hire the past two years (Washington and Oregon). He accounted for a combined 41 passes defended over the past three seasons (no other player had more than 34). With his full-ﬁeld awareness, Muhammad shows the innate ability to judge the catch point and make plays on the football. He has the gritty play style needed for the move inside to the nickel, although that also would shine a light on some of his warts as a run defender. Overall, Muhammad has arguably the most impressive blend of ﬂuidity and ball-hawking instincts in this draft class, but masking his size, speed and strength limitations will be a tough task against NFL-caliber athletes. His NFL-ready skill set will give him a chance to stand out in camp.

name: Fentrell Cypress II
summary: Fentrell Cypress II grew up in Virginia (Newport News and Petersburg) before moving to South Carolina at age 11. He played wide receiver and cornerback at Northwestern High in Rock Hill, combining for 59 passes defended and six interceptions over his ﬁnal two seasons (also had a 10.70-second 100-meter time in track). THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 462 A three-star recruit, Cypress signed with Virginia and had a breakout fourth season in 2022. He transferred to Florida State for his ﬁnal two seasons and posted 12 passes defended over 23 starts. Cypress is a height-length-speed prospect with the athleticism in space to mirror, ﬂoat and maintain relationships between multiple routes. He drives on passes well in zone coverage to get his hands on the football without making early contact (zero penalties at Florida State), although his low interception number is discouraging. He's too much of a "catch" tackler, but he gets his guy on the ground. Overall, Cypress hasn't put consistency on tape, but when you grade to the ﬂashes and trust his testing numbers, you can understand why a team could think there might be something there.

name: Jermari Harris
strengths: ● Good-sized athlete with decent length ● Pattern matches smoothly from zone ● Stays dialed in with his eyes to ﬂoat and make plays ● Baits throws from different levels to enter passing lane late ● Physical at the top of routes and quick to regain positioning ● Addresses the ball well with strong hand-eye coordination to ﬁnish interceptions ● Strikes like a ton of bricks when he locks on to his target ● Plays with an edge, which helps him escape perimeter blocks ● Quality ball production as a three-year starter

summary: A three-year starter at Iowa, Harris was the left cornerback in defensive coordinator Phil Parker's 4-2-5 base scheme, playing heavy doses of Cover 2. His career with the Hawkeyes was marred by several setbacks (2022 injury; gambling suspension), but his on-ﬁeld play improved each season — he allowed just 16 catches with 10 passes defended and zero penalties in 2024. Harris sees the ﬁeld well from off coverage to anticipate catch windows and put himself in position to make plays on the football. He is a little tight in his pedal and will struggle if asked to man up against route technicians who can lose his trail. Overall, Harris won't be an ideal ﬁt for every scheme and needs to be more dependable as a tackler, but his instincts and competitive proﬁle will have zone-heavy teams interested. Pre-draft interviews will be paramount to his ﬁnal grade.

name: Isas Waxter II
summary: Isas (ice-iss) "Ice" Waxter II grew up in the Newark, N.J., area with his mother (Glenda). He started playing football and running track at age 8. He attended Immaculate Conception High and played both ways (cornerback and wide receiver). A no-star recruit, Waxter received seven FCS offers and committed to Villanova. After missing the 2022 season because of a knee injury, he became a full-time starter the past two seasons and led the CAA with three forced fumbles in 2024. Waxter is a good-sized athlete who looks to disrupt routes early. He works hard to stay on top of the route, although his handsy approach won't ﬂy against NFL athletes. He doesn't shy from the physicality in the run game, but he must ﬁnd better control to cut down on missed tackles. Overall, Waxter needs to polish his footwork and technique, but he passes the eye test, runs well enough and battles on every snap. Some NFL teams have him tagged as a future safety.

name: Ethan Robinson
summary: Louis Ethan Robinson was born in Bronxville, N.Y., with his parents (Louis and Tawanda). A basketball-focused athlete as a kid, he also grew up playing quarterback before switching to the secondary at Iona Prep. A three-year starter, he posted 30 tackles and one interception as a junior in 2019. A no-star recruit, he received only FCS offers and committed to Bucknell over several Ivy League programs. He started immediately and had a breakout season as a junior. He jumped into the transfer portal after the 2023 season and received more than 20 offers from schools in the SEC, Big Ten and other conferences before choosing Minnesota. He started at outside cornerback for the Gophers and earned All-Big Ten honors in 2024. Though his recovery speed is lacking, Robinson has good feet and a natural understanding of route combinations to put himself in position to make plays. Overall, Robinson has strong off-man coverage skills, and the FCS-to-FBS jump wasn't too big for him. He projects best as a Cover 2 corner with ball skills and toughness.

name: BJ Mayes
summary: Brian "BJ" Mayes grew up in Houston's Third Ward with his parents (Brian and Sheila). He was primarily a cornerback at Houston Heights High and combined for four interceptions (one pick six) over his junior and senior years. A three-star recruit, Mayes was committed to UTSA for eight months, but the school ran out of scholarship spots and he was left scrambling the week before signing day. He played at FCS Incarnate Word for two seasons before jumping up to the FBS with UAB in 2023. Mayes later transferred again, joining Mike Elko's ﬁrst recruiting class at Texas A&M for the 2024 season. Primarily an outside cornerback, he moved inside to the nickel at Texas A&M and did a nice job balancing his eyes between the route and the quarterback to break on the football (led the Aggies with four interceptions). He has decent size for the position but is inconsistent as a tackler and leaks yardage. Overall, Mayes lacks quick twitch in his movements, which leaves him making excessive contact mid-route. For better or worse, though, he is the type of defensive back who trusts his athletic instincts to put himself in position to make plays.

name: Melvin Smith Jr.
summary: Melvin Smith Jr. grew up in northwest Louisiana and started playing football in elementary school. He was an all-league defensive back as a senior at Airline High in Bossier City, leading the program to a 10-win season and the 2019 district title. A no-star recruit, he signed with Division II Southern Arkansas, where he became a four-year starter. He had proliﬁc junior and senior seasons, registering a combined 35 passes defended and nine interceptions. Smith has production that jumps off the page — and it came both in off coverage, where he could drive on throws, and press man, where he pinned receivers to the sideline and found the football. He is only average in his hip turn and can get stuck at times in his transitions, but he plays with heart. I also don't question his compete skills, although his tackling was average, even by Division II standards, and must improve for him to get NFL athletes on the ground. Overall, Smith had the pre-draft process he needed to earn a shot — he didn't appear out of his element against better competition at the Senior Bowl, and his testing veriﬁed that he has NFL-level athleticism.

name: Trikweze Bridges
summary: Trikweze (TRY-kwez) Bridges, one of three kids, grew up in Lanett, Ala. Several of his relatives played college football, including his father (Tremayne), who was a wide receiver at Florida A&M. At Lanett High, Bridges earned all-state honors three straight years and as a junior safety (104 tackles, 10 interceptions) and receiver led the team to the 2017 Class 1A state championship. He also led the basketball team to multiple state titles (his mother, Marcilyn Patrick, is a former basketball player). A three-star recruit, he spurned several SEC offers (including one from Alabama) to sign with Oregon. After ﬁve years in Eugene, he transferred to the SEC for his super-senior season. He came off the bench early before becoming a starting safety and then a corner, leading the Gators in tackles and allowing just 14 catches (no touchdowns) in 2024. THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 466 An impressive athlete for his size, Bridges can press and use his impressive length to reroute receivers. He closes distance well from off coverage and arrives with physicality. Overall, Bridges has the tools and versatility to match up with size at receiver, and his impressive testing likely guaranteed him a long look in an NFL training camp.

name: O'Donnell Fortune
summary: O'Donnell Fortune started playing football in ﬁfth grade for the Chargers at Dillon Park in Sumter, S.C. His junior year at Sumter High put him on the recruiting map (ﬁve interceptions — he had three more as a senior and received all-state honors). Fortune was a three-star recruit as a safety and corner and grew up a Gamecocks fan. After a 100-yard pick six in South Carolina's 2022 bowl game, he became a starter as a junior and played his best ball as a senior. Fortune is a tall, slender athlete with length that he uses to disrupt route timing and obstruct passing windows. He isn't shy about trusting his instincts and tracking the eyes of the quarterback to make plays. His tackling was ﬁne on some tapes but atrocious on others (LSU, Illinois, Kentucky), especially when he tried to hit too high. Overall, Fortune needs to play with improved discipline, both in coverage and run support, but his ball awareness and ﬂuidity will translate well to the pro game.

name: Jalen Kimber
summary: Jalen "Boogie" Kimber, one of four kids, grew up in Chicago with his parents (Art and Lisa) before the family relocated to Texas. He played both corner and safety at Mansﬁeld Timberview High and collected two interceptions as a junior. A four-star recruit, his recruitment skyrocketed after his testing at The Opening Regional camp, and he later committed to Georgia. THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 467 After his 2021 season ended because of a shoulder surgery, Kimber entered the portal and transferred to Florida, where he played two seasons. For his ﬁnal season, he again entered the portal, this time committing to Louisville before ﬂipping to Penn State, where he won an outside corner starting spot. Kimber is a lean-framed athlete and lacks ideal functional strength to reroute physical receivers. His lack of ball instincts downﬁeld also shows on tape, but he can turn and run vertically, showing ﬂuid body control to stay in phase. Despite his lack of size, he was a sound tackler on the 2024 tape. Overall, Kimber needs to play with better poise in coverage, but he has the athletic talent to keep up with NFL receivers and compete for a role on special teams.

name: Donte Kent
summary: Donte Kent grew up in Harrisburg, Pa., with his parents (Ronald and Kathy). He was a two-way star (wide receiver and cornerback) at Harrisburg High and combined for 10 interceptions over his junior and senior seasons. A three-star recruit, he received mostly MAC offers and committed to Central Michigan. He compiled almost as many passes defended (47) as starts (48) over the past ﬁve seasons. As a senior, he added punt return duties to his resume and averaged 13.6 yards per return, including a 68-yard touchdown. Playing a lot of Cover 2, Kent skillfully uses his eyes to pick up on route clues and drive on throws. His aggressiveness can get him in trouble at times, but he shows the make-up speed on tape to recover. Despite getting his hands on a lot of footballs, he was able to convert only two passes into turnovers. Overall, Kent is an above-average tackler for the position (at least 50 tackles each of the past four years) with NFL-quality speed, processing and special teams value.

name: Nikko Reed
summary: Nikko Reed was born in San Francisco and raised by his mother (Maria Napitan). His older brother (Khalil Hudson) played wide receiver at Southern Oregon. Reed played wide receiver and corner at Moreau Catholic High and collected 2,199 career all-purpose yards and 13 interceptions (three returned for touchdowns). An undersized (155 pounds) three-star recruit, he committed to Colorado, his lone then-Power 5 offer. After starting in 2022, he was part of the program's max exodus that came after Deion Sanders took the head-coaching job and ﬂipped the roster. Reed transferred to Oregon and became arguably the Ducks' most consistent starter in 2024. He is light-footed with balanced movement skills and recovery speed. His pattern recognition has shown steady improvements, although you'd like to see him better anticipate break points to be more disruptive. Overall, Reed lacks ideal size and explosiveness, but he plays ﬂuid and natural in reverse and is quick to support the run. He's a candidate for a nickel role.

name: Zemaiah Vaughn
summary: Zemaiah (zuh-my-uh) Vaughn, one of eight children, grew up in southeast Texas, with his parents (Chris and Zipporah). Following in one of his older brother's footsteps, he grew up playing quarterback and earned ﬁrst-team all-district honors in 2019 as a senior at United High (1,049 rushing yards and 854 passing yards). A no-star recruit, he was overlooked until Utah and defensive coordinator Morgan Scalley gave him a walk-on opportunity as a defensive back. Despite having no experience in the secondary, he joined the Utes and made the positional transition, eventually starting 31 straight games at left cornerback to ﬁnish his career. Although leaner than is ideal, Vaughn has an elite mix of height, length and straight-line speed. He is leggy in his movements — some of that stiffness hinders his ability to stay attached with quick-twitch route runners. He entered the 2024 season with high expectations, but offenses found too much success throwing at his side of the ﬁeld. Overall, Vaughn allows too much separation in man, but he is long and fast and has upside as a corner in Cover 3, where he could read and react.

name: Jordan Clark
summary: Jordan Clark, who has two sisters, grew up in Baton Rouge, La., with his parents (Ryan and Yonka). His father put together a 13-year NFL career (2002-14) at defensive back, mostly with the Pittsburgh Steelers, despite going undrafted out of LSU (Ryan Clark is now an NFL analyst for ESPN). Jordan Clark developed a love for football and told his father in eighth grade that he eventually wanted to play college ball. He became an All-America defensive back at University Lab School in Baton Rouge. A four-star recruit, he committed to Arizona State, where he lined up primarily as a nickel over ﬁve years in Tempe. Clark transferred to Notre Dame for his ﬁnal season and was part of the nickel rotation in Al Golden's scheme, helping the Irish reach the national title game. He is very smooth in his movements and doesn't look out of his depth with man-coverage duties. He shows hip snap as a tackler, although his technique can be buttoned up to help him be a more consistent ﬁnisher. Overall, Clark is a ﬂuid athlete with a nose for the football. NFL teams speak highly about his interviews and intangibles.

name: Dontae Manning
summary: Dontae Manning grew up in the Kansas City, Mo., area and was a standout basketball, football and track athlete at Raytown High. He played on all three phases for the football team and earned ﬁrst-team all-state honors as a senior with 970 rushing yards, 97 tackles and 24 total touchdowns. He also set school track records of 10.67 seconds in the 100 meters and 22.27 in the 200. A ﬁve-star recruit, he was a consensus top-ﬁve corner in his class and originally committed to Oklahoma before ﬂipping to Oregon. He struggled to separate himself as a full-time starter and spent most of his career as a nickel/dime outside corner (22.8 defensive snaps per game in 2024). He was able to make an impact as a senior as a core-four special-teamer (216 special teams snaps in 2024). Manning has electric speed but lacks fundamental transition ability to stay attached to routes. His anticipation and feel for concepts are still in the development phase. Overall, Manning doesn't have draftable tape on defense, but he offers a combination of rare length, athletic gifts and special teams experience that makes him worth bringing to training camp.

name: Kam Alexander
summary: Kameryn "Kam" Alexander grew up outside of Houston and was a standout football and track athlete at Manvel High. He was an all-district cornerback as a senior and had personal bests of 22 feet, 7 inches in the long jump and 46-1 in the triple jump. A no-star recruit, he signed with Sam Houston State and helped the program win the FCS championship in the spring of 2021. He transferred up to UTSA in 2023 and ﬁnished top ﬁve in the FBS in passes defended (17) in 2023. Again looking to challenge himself, he transferred to Oregon in 2024 but failed to win a starting job and played just 71 defensive snaps in a Ducks uniform. Alexander plays fast and competitive, with springs in his calves to explode downhill. However, his awareness and reaction skills are undisciplined and take him out of position. His underpowered frame shows against bigger receivers and when tackling bully runners. Overall, Alexander wasn't able to translate his 2023 success to his play for the Ducks in 2024, but his top-tier athletic traits were on display at his pro day, which will force NFL teams to take a longer look.

name: TJ Moore
summary: Tremain "TJ" Moore, one of four children, grew up in Riverdale, Ga., with his parents (Tamyra Smith and Tremain Sr.). He played both ways as a corner, wide receiver and quarterback at Riverdale High. A no-star recruit, he received mostly Division II interest (primarily at receiver) until FCS Mercer entered the mix. Moore signed there to play defense and immediately claimed a role as part of the secondary rotation, playing in 59 games (including 56 straight) over the past ﬁve seasons. He became just the second unanimous All-American in school history in 2024 (20 passes defended and seven interceptions). A good-sized athlete, Moore maintains good positioning in zone and aggressively plays the football with timing (zero penalties in 2024). He ﬂashes a burst to close in coverage and run support, although his attempts to bait throws will backﬁre at times, and you'd like to see more disciplined technique. Overall, Moore will get in trouble freelancing, but he is a twitched-up athlete with physicality and ball skills. He will have a chance to compete for an NFL roster spot.

summary: A three-year starter at South Carolina, Emmanwori was listed as a free safety on the depth chart in defensive coordinator Clayton White's ﬂex-nickel scheme, but he lined up primarily in the box with some slot and deep snaps. Because of injuries on the Gamecocks' roster, he was thrust into the starting lineup as a true freshman and became the program's ﬁrst defender since Jadeveon Clowney to earn freshman All-American honors. After leading the team in tackles in 2022, he did it again as a junior and was one of only three FBS players with multiple pick sixes in 2024. Emmanwori does a nice job reading route concepts in underneath coverages, and he will make plays on the ball with his reaction quickness. Some of his reads and angles are inconsistent from depth, but he keys quickly from the box and plays with physicality (Derwin James is his idol). Overall, Emmanwori has the size, speed and mindset to play a variety of roles, although he projects best near the line of scrimmage, where he can blitz, be an eraser against the run and man up with tight ends and backs in coverage. He has the ﬂoor of an adequate starter and special-teamer, but his ceiling is exciting and will put him high on NFL teams' safety stack.

summary: A three-year starter at Georgia, Starks was a do-everything safety (post, split-ﬁeld, box, slot) in head coach Kirby Smart's man/zone scheme, often playing the "Star" nickel position. After announcing himself as a playmaker in his ﬁrst game as a true freshman, he became a ﬁxture of the Bulldogs secondary and earned All-America honors each of his three seasons. He quickly established himself as one of Georgia's leaders, both as a worker behind the scenes and on the ﬁeld, often getting his teammates lined up properly based on offensive adjustments. With his length, athleticism and recognition skills, Starks is a strong space defender and plays conﬁdent in all aspects of coverage and run support. Though there are plenty of examples of his range and playmaking skills, he doesn't consistently position himself to be disruptive in man-to-man situations — that issue led to several big plays allowed in 2024. Overall, Starks doesn't have Teﬂon tape, especially in man coverage, but his athletic proﬁle, diagnose skills and intangibles will make him an immediate starter and special-teamer in the NFL. His versatile skill set can give a defensive coordinator options, although he is best suited for a free safety role.

summary: A two-year starter at Notre Dame, Watts played the ﬁeld safety position in former defensive coordinator Al Golden's 4-2-5 base scheme, lining up mostly two-high and in the box, with one-high and slot reps. After toiling on offense upon his arrival in South Bend, he moved to rover linebacker before ﬁnding his home at free safety, where he became one of the most decorated players in Irish history. He collected 13 combined interceptions (and allowed zero touchdown catches) over the past two seasons, becoming the ﬁrst two-time consensus All-American at Notre Dame since 1993. Without imposing size or high-level explosiveness, Watts has been a slow-burn evaluation for NFL scouts, but his playmaking instincts are indisputable on tape. Although his aggressive nature leads to occasional mistakes, he plays with a quick, decisive trigger and his tone-setting toughness pops versus both run and pass. Overall, Watts isn't a safety you want playing man-to-man coverage against slot receivers very often, but he is a solid run defender with the route anticipation and ball skills to sniff out plays from depth. He projects as an NFL starter and would ﬁt best in a split-safety, zone-heavy scheme, in which he can play two-deep and underneath zone.

However, you could still spot his offensive roots, as he was responsible for four defensive touchdowns (with an average return of 58 yards) over the past two seasons. With his range, ﬂuidity and post-snap diagnosing skills, Bowman anticipates well in coverage to drive and ﬁnish at the football, and he's a threat to score every time he touches the ball. Though physical in run support, he is often overzealous with his angles and ﬁnish, and his small margin for error as a tackler leads to negative results. A former high school quarterback in eight-man football, he blossomed over his ﬁnal two seasons with the Cavaliers, leading the ACC in solo tackles in both 2023 (73) and 2024 (65). Sanker is guilty of arriving too hot at times, which leaves him late to break down in the alley, but he is a long, rangy tackler who runs through the ball carrier to ﬁnish. Although some question his ability to make plays on the ball in coverage, he reads route stems well in underneath zone and can match tight ends in man-to-man to break on throws before they leave the quarterback's hand. Overall, Sanker will be well-liked by NFL coaches because of his natural athleticism, competitive urgency and intangibles, as well as his strong special teams proﬁle. He projects best as an instinctive box safety.

Although he made a name for himself as a freshman All-American at Clemson, he put inconsistent play on tape as a sophomore and junior nickel after Brent Venables left the program. Considered at that point a borderline draft pick, he transferred to Austin for his senior year and played the best ball of his career, giving a boost to his projection. Mukuba is at his best ﬂying through alleys with urgency and conviction, but also with enough control to course correct angles while at full speed to leverage the run. He plays bigger than he looks, but he has mediocre ﬁnishing strength and some teams are worried about long-term durability because of his aggressive play style. Despite an average athletic proﬁle, he is quick to read run/pass and shows terriﬁc discipline in coverage (18 passes defended, zero penalties over his ﬁnal 26 games in college). Overall, Mukuba's lack of size will be more noticeable against NFL competition, both in coverage and run support, but he brings energy, instincts and play speed to the secondary. He has the mentality and talent to compete for a starting role at free safety.

Because of his range, Ransom is at his best making noise in the run game with read-and-drive quickness and high-speed collision tackles — he creates bug-meet-windshield hits from different angles. After Branch left for the NFL, Moore was up and down as a nickel in Saban's defense in 2023, but he moved to more of a traditional safety role in 2024 and produced his best season. Although you don't want him consistently playing man-to-man coverage against NFL wide receivers, Moore does have the coverage awareness to put himself in position to make plays. He is a very willing run defender, and teams will love the competitive edge he brings to the ﬁeld. Overall, Moore doesn't have difference-making size or athletic traits, but he is a tough, instinctive player who can defend the run and play with just enough range in coverage. weaknesses: ● Doesn't stand out — on paper or in pads — in terms of size or length ● Quality speed, but he'll have a tough time if asked to cover slot receivers in man coverage ● Better anticipation will help him squeeze routes ● Falls off tackle attempts occasionally because of his lack of ideal measurements ● Minimal reps as a blitzer (didn't have any career sacks) ● Missed one game as junior because of hamstring injury (Oct. 2023); missed two games with injuries as senior (Oct. 2024)
summary: A three-year starter at Maryland, Trader primarily played a ﬁeld safety role in defensive coordinator Brian Williams' balanced scheme, alternating from the post or walking down toward the line. A former top-ﬁve recruit in lacrosse, he was a dual-sport athlete for most of his life — including with the Terrapins — and will beneﬁt from being 100 percent focused on football in the NFL. With his urgent, competitive mentality, Trader has twitchy responses to plays in front of him and loves to be around the action. His long speed isn't as impressive as his short-area burst, which can lead to coverage lapses if his reads aren't on point. Overall, Trader falls short of what teams desire size-wise at safety, but he is a tough, instinctive defender at his best driving downhill, although he also can patrol the deep half and match up man-to-man against tight ends. His aggressive play style will help him earn a backup role with the potential to eventually become a starter.

name: Marques Sigle
strengths: ● Former cornerback and hasn't lost that speed ● His 15.13 mph at ﬁve yards during his 40-yard dash was combine's fastest ● Plays with patience when reading and reacting to receiver movements ● Smooth pedal and turn when manning up in the slot ● Disciplined process to track eyes of the quarterback to throwing lanes ● Didn't commit a coverage penalty in 2024 ● Rangy run defender with speed to opposite edge ● Widens his base and strikes belt of the ball carrier as tackler ● Voted a senior captain, and NFL scouts speak highly of his standing in the program ● Didn't have much of a special teams role at Kansas State, but was a core special-teamer at North Dakota State (combined 12 tackles in 2021-22)
weaknesses: ● A tad light for safety work, with mediocre ﬁnishing strength ● Average anticipation from depth and can get overly conservative reading keys ● Must sharpen up coverage angles ● Strong tackling form, but misses are usually a result of lunging prematurely or not getting arms wrapped in time ● Average length and shock in hands when attempting to take on bodies ● Physical blockers will keep him occupied
summary: A two-year starter at Kansas State, Sigle was a hybrid nickel safety in defensive coordinator Joe Klanderman's balanced scheme and rotated between free, strong, nickel and dime safety. A cornerback at North Dakota State, he transferred to Kansas State for his ﬁnal two college seasons, earned a starting role and led the team in interceptions as a senior (including a 43-yard pick six versus West Virginia). In coverage, Sigle is rangy playing over the top and in slot man, although some of his tardy reactions create throwing windows. Despite being a tad undersized for downhill duties, he is bursty in the run game with the trigger and tackling mechanics to get his man on the ground. Overall, Sigle's missteps can be costly, but he feels route development around him and has above-average speed to be a factor in the play. He is scheme versatile with the athleticism to ﬁt different coverages.

name: Hunter Wohler
strengths: ● Good-sized athlete with motor and edge that stand out to scouts ● Outstanding run-diagnose skills and quickly puts himself on the right path ● Gears down smoothly to easily redirect pursuit (posted top three-cone time at combine) ● Plays physical through contact in the box ● Matches up well with tight ends and backs in man-to-man ● Crowds airspace well but was ﬂagged for only two pass interference penalties over 25 college starts ● NFL scouts describe him as a "coach's dream" because of his belief in the program and hatred for losing ● Experienced on special teams coverages (also averaged nine yards per return as backup punt returner) ● His 120 tackles in 2023 were most by a Wisconsin defensive back since 1991
weaknesses: ● Speed is solid but doesn't jump out as a differentiating trait ● Middling twitch in open ﬁeld and will stumble in his click and close ● Often ﬁnds himself in and out of phase and needs to stay in the hip pocket ● Questionable deep-third range when attempting to play the sideline ● No interceptions on 2024 tape ● Short arms, which will leave him stuck on blocks near the line ● Broken left ﬁbula suffered in 2022 season opener (his ﬁrst career start) and missed next seven games; knocked out of Oregon game (Nov. 2024) and missed the following game
summary: A two-year starter at Wisconsin, Wohler lined up at strong safety in defensive coordinator Mike Tressel's 2-4-5 base scheme. He led the Badgers in tackles each of his two seasons as a starter, and the defense looked completely different in the one game he missed in 2024. Despite his short arms, Wohler is automatic as a tackler with his ability to work down, wrap and ﬁnish one-on-one (averaged eight tackles per game over the past two seasons). He shows some promise covering in underneath zones, but savvy route runners can get him turned around, and his recovery skills are mediocre. Overall, Wohler is a one-speed athlete and will be limited as a true coverage player at the next level, but his read-react ability and competitive edge versus the run should give him NFL value. He might not be an ideal starter, but he has the tools to hang around as a quality depth piece and special-teamer.

name: Sebastian Castro
strengths: ● His best athletic trait is ﬂuid balance for smooth transitions ● Plays with urgency in his key and drive to make stops at the line of scrimmage in run game ● Fast and sharp downhill angles raise chances of ﬁnishing open-ﬁeld tackles ● Physical ﬁnisher; throws body into the lower half of ball carrier (grew up idolizing Troy Polamalu) ● Gauges play speed from depth to leverage the ﬁeld and guard the sticks ● Anticipates well from zone to undercut routes ● Big, steady hands to pick off inaccurate throws ● Didn't commit a coverage penalty over past two seasons (26 games) ● Detailed work ethic instilled in him at a young age by his grandfather
weaknesses: ● Not a special athlete, with average-at-best speed ● More controlled than sudden in open-ﬁeld movements ● Inconsistent as a true man-to-man defender ● Managed just two passes defended in 2024 (ninth on the Hawkeyes) ● Eagerness to make plays as senior led to false steps ● Arrives too hot at times as tackler and gets caught between wrapping and striking ● Didn't play on punt coverage in college ● Will be 25 as a rookie THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 497
summary: A three-year starter at Iowa, Castro played the nickel "Cash" position in defensive coordinator Phil Parker's 4-2-5 base scheme, lining up primarily as a hybrid slot/linebacker. He earned draftable grades from NFL scouts after his All-American 2023 season, but his super-senior season was somewhat disappointing — he had more touchdowns allowed in coverage (ﬁve) than passes defended (two). Iowa has developed a reputation for sending alert, competitive and opportunistic defensive backs to the league, and Castro is next up in the pipeline. Though not a top-tier athlete, he is a smooth, decisive player who keys well and takes smart angles in zone coverage and run support. Overall, Castro is an instinctive zone defender with trustworthy football character, but his ordinary speed and explosiveness limit his upside in most schemes. He best ﬁts as a big nickel safety, likely as a backup.

name: Dan Jackson
strengths: ● Plays with a decisive reactor for quick-drive triggers ● Forceful high-to-low tackler — runs the alley like a runaway train ● Looks to lay licks on crossers and screens ● Anticipates wide receiver breaks and gets a head start THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 498 ● Forced key fumble late against Georgia Tech in his ﬁnal game in Athens, which allowed Bulldogs to come back and win (Nov. 2024) ● Extensive special teams background and a regular on kickoff and punt return coverage the past four seasons (blocked ﬁeld goal in 2024) ● Described as "phenomenal" teammate because of a positive attitude and work ethic that raises the bar (Smart: "All he does is give everything he's got every single day.") ● Only missed start in 2024 was because of a targeting penalty the week before
weaknesses: ● Average frame and lacks ideal length ● Tight hips and inconsistent sink create lags in redirects ● Lackluster coverage speed, especially when defending the sidelines ● Bites on initial route movements and can be fooled by ball/head fakes ● Misses too many tackles when he arrives too hot ● Tackling technique leaves plenty to be desired — often hits instead of wrapping ● Stress fracture in foot (Oct. 2022), which required season-ending surgery (also missed 2023 spring practices) ● Only one season playing starter snaps ● Will turn 25 during his rookie season
summary: A one-year starter at Georgia, Jackson was a versatile safety in head coach Kirby Smart's scheme, lining up in two-high and in middle-ﬁeld cheat coverage. Despite not being recruited by the Bulldogs, he earned his way as a walk-on and played six seasons without a football scholarship, becoming an impactful starter in 2024 (Smart admits they "lucked into" having him). When he keeps the play in front of him, Jackson reacts without hesitation and closes with an extra gear to explode through contact. Though the highlights are ﬁreworks, he also has reckless tendencies because of his aggressive play style. He must introduce more discipline into his tackling process. Overall, Jackson doesn't have the high-end coverage skills desired at the position, but he is instinctive, tough and determined, and his stopwatch speed shows when working downhill. At the very least, his special teams impact will make it tough for an NFL coaching staff to cut him.

name: Craig Woodson
strengths: ● Controlled, ﬂuid mover and stays on the same plan vertically in his turn and run ● Has good feel for spacing in the deep third to inﬂuence multiple routes ● Good timing when attacking the catch point to dislodge ball from man ● Arrives without going through receivers (one coverage penalty over past three seasons) ● Accelerates through hips of ball carrier as tackler ● Productive playing down at line of scrimmage ● Stopwatch speed shows up most as a backside chaser ● Plenty of special teams experience (450 career snaps) ● Started all 38 games the past three seasons; NFL scouts say he is an A-plus person
weaknesses: ● More smooth than dynamic in his movements ● Trusts his eyes but can be manipulated for that very reason ● Plays with good speed but not good enough to easily recover from a misstep ● Needs to eliminate zigs and zags from pursuit angles ● Required season-ending surgery after injuring knee during 2021 fall camp ● Will be 24 on draft weekend
summary: A three-year starter at Cal, Woodson was an interchangeable safety in head coach Justin Wilcox's 2-4-5 base scheme, playing nickel and both the ﬁeld and boundary spots. He had a tough ﬁrst three years in Berkeley (redshirt, COVID-19, knee injury), but he was a consistent presence over his ﬁnal three seasons and got better each year, which didn't go unnoticed by NFL scouts. Whether playing down or on the backend, Woodson shows terriﬁc recognition of run-pass development to smartly put himself in positions to make plays. He is at his best in short zones or split-safety alignments, where he can maintain spacing and drive on the football. Overall, Woodson doesn't have dominant size or traits that make him jump off the ﬁlm, but he is good enough in most critical categories NFL teams want at the safety position. He will be ready from day one to compete for a depth role.

name: Rayuan Lane III
strengths: ● Explosive lower body for sudden drives on the football ● Displays twitch in movements to avoid blocks or react with route runners ● Reaches landmarks with ease in coverage and baits the quarterback ● Created combined 11 turnovers over past two seasons (six interceptions, ﬁve forced fumbles) ● Can see his offensive background on interception tries (both pick sixes were longer than 86 yards) ● Fearless as run defender ● Makes defensive checks and communicates well to get teammates lined up ● Durable and versatile — ﬁnished career with 43 straight starts (NFL scout: "His coaches say he never even missed practice.") ● Shined as a gunner all four seasons (23 career special teams tackles)
weaknesses: ● Frame and length won't be selling points in draft rooms ● Fills quickly but will overcommit himself and create tougher angles ● Physical ball carriers can power through his wrap-catch attempts (see 2024 Tulane tape) ● Doesn't have ideal speed to keep stride with NFL receivers ● Can get grabby when out of position (four pass interference ﬂags in 2024, including one that brought back an interception on the Temple tape) ● Three personal foul penalties as senior
summary: A four-year starter at Navy, Lane was a versatile safety in head coach Brian Newberry's 4-2-5 base scheme, which showcased his versatility across the secondary. After he went overlooked as a high school recruit, he became a freshman starter for the Midshipmen and bypassed transfer opportunities to create his legacy at Navy. An instinctive athlete, Lane sees the ﬁeld well and understands where the quarterback wants to go, showing a feel for when to roll the dice. He trusts his eyes to drive on plays in front of him, although his timing and break-down technique can be improved. Overall, Lane needs to improve his reliability ﬁnishing tackles, but his ﬂuid athleticism and football IQ are NFL-quality traits. His special teams impact as a gunner can really separate him on draft boards and in training camp.

name: Malik Verdon
strengths: ● Frame and length that immediately draw the eye ● Smooth movements in short areas for quick reactions ● Drives on targets from short zone ● Uses length to disrupt throws near his air space and force incompletions ● Active to be where he needs to be supporting the run ● Pursuit effort is consistent to chase down runners ● Not shy delivering jarring hits near line of scrimmage ● Played penalty-free football in college (zero career ﬂags)
weaknesses: ● Lean-muscled with little deﬁnition on his frame ● Average speed player who quickly ﬁnds himself out-angled ● Can react with the play but doesn't consistently anticipate ● Hard to feel great about his man-coverage feel ● Too many missed tackles, usually because his upper-body strength wasn't enough to ﬁnish ● Didn't play on any kickoff or punt coverages in college ● Missed ﬁnal nine games of 2022 season after undergoing season-ending surgery (Oct. 2022); missed three games as sophomore because of hairline fracture in left forearm (Oct. 2023); missed time as senior with left hand injury (Oct. 2024) and wore club over ﬁnal month of season; right shoulder surgery (March 2025) after Iowa State's pro day (expected to be cleared for training camp)
summary: A two-year starter at Iowa State, Verdon lined up as the boundary safety in defensive coordinator Jon Heacock's zone-heavy scheme, spending most of his time in the box or over the slot. Primarily a quarterback in high school, he battled injuries over his last three seasons, but his impact and tackle production still increased each year. Verdon has the body length and smooth athleticism to match up in man and zone coverage, although he tends to be more reactive than proactive. Though not an intimidating or forceful tackler, he stays disciplined with his keys and does a nice job lassoing ball carriers. Overall, Verdon is a tall, long athlete with a unique skill set as a low-hole defender, but his anticipation and ﬁnishing skills must improve before he is ready for full-time snaps in the NFL. Learning to make an impact on special teams will be important for him.

name: Kitan Crawford
strengths: ● Athletic testing created buzz at the combine ● Both fast and agile, which leads to quick on-ﬁeld reactions ● Eye balance to read the quarterback and route runner appeared to improve throughout the season ● Flashes intercepting skills on balls thrown near him ● Doesn't back down when asked to cover tight ends ● Not shy about mixing things up as a run defender ● Extensive special teams experience (1,010 career snaps) ● Special teams resume in college: 17 tackles, 10 penalties, one blocked ﬁeld goal and one blocked punt
weaknesses: ● Only one full season of starting experience ● Doesn't always move at full speed if he doesn't trust what he is seeing ● Savvy route runners can get him turned around ● Play-action pass can lure him down ● Inconsistent coming to balance as tackler — will be too hot or out of position ● Average play strength; needs to improve taking on and shedding stalk blocks
summary: A one-year starter at Nevada, Crawford played free safety while rotating in the box and as a nickel in head coach Jeff Choate's multiple coverage looks. Highly recruited out of East Texas, he made an impact on special teams for the Longhorns but struggled to break through on defense. He transferred to Nevada in 2024 for the opportunity to be an every-down safety. THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 503 Crawford is a ﬂuid, loose athlete who can unlock and play fast to the football, although he can be moved off his post and often reacts to the ﬁrst look from the quarterback. There aren't any questions about his willingness as a run defender, but his reliability ﬁnishing tackles must improve. Overall, Crawford has NFL-level speed and athleticism, but his inconsistent reads reﬂect his meager starting experience in the secondary. His special teams background and testing numbers will make him an appealing prospect in the later rounds.

name: R.J. Mickens
strengths: ● Solidly built with quality length ● Appeared leaner and quicker in 2024 compared to underclassman tape ● Drives downhill and widens feet to break down and ﬁnish tackles ● Physical in run support, getting low and sticking his pads into the gut of gap runners ● Smoothly turns with tight ends and receivers out of the break ● Reads quarterback's eyes from depth, with instincts to jump passes ● Productive player on the ball — wide receiver background shows (had a pick six called back by penalty in playoff game versus Texas) ● Named a team captain in 2024 and was recognized as a P.A.W. Journey ambassador (unique leadership) ● Played on punt return coverages all ﬁve seasons THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 504
weaknesses: ● Solid yet unspectacular athlete ● Mediocre speed in coverage and will give up separation on crossers or vertical shots ● Lacks suddenness in recovery attempts ● Wasn't ﬂagged in 2024, but he got away with grabs in coverage, especially deep (see 2024 Georgia tape) ● Misses in the run game usually came when he left his feet too early
summary: A three-year starter at Clemson, Mickens played a versatile safety role in former defensive coordinator Wes Goodwin's scheme, aligning at free safety, nickel and near the box. He made the most of his ﬁnal season, ﬁnishing third on the team in tackles (85) and second in interceptions (two). The son of an 11-year NFL veteran, Mickens grew up around the game, and it shows in the way he sees the ﬁeld — especially when working from depth in the run game as a willing, secure tackler. In coverage, he is more smooth than sudden with his movements and trusts his instincts to lead him to the catch point. Overall, Mickens doesn't consistently play up to his testing numbers, but he has a keen sense of football geometry and takes precise, physical angles to the football. He projects as a potential backup and special-teamer in the NFL.

name: Alijah Clark
strengths: ● Versatile experience across the secondary ● Will go up and high point the ball — his offensive background is evident ● Reads well from depth, with a feel for developing routes ● Physical in coverage to disrupt timing at break points ● Flies downhill in the run game and looks to face-up runners in the hole ● His default setting as a striker is "violent" ● Played on punt coverages in college
weaknesses: ● Physically, looks more like a corner than a safety ● Limited hip ﬂexibility in space ● Freelancing footwork needs continued polish ● Might struggle against the agility of NFL receivers, especially in the slot ● Overaggressive tendencies in run ﬁlls and doesn't give himself much room for error (see 2024 Virginia Tech tape) ● Unnecessary roughness ﬂag on 2024 Boston College tape (Boston College scored touchdown two plays later) ● Served partial one-game suspension as junior (Nov. 2023) for violation of team rules (played on special teams but not defense)
summary: A three-year starter at Syracuse, Clark was an interchangeable safety in defensive coordinator Elijah Robinson's scheme, splitting time evenly between nickel, ﬁeld and boundary roles. After one year at Rutgers, he jumped to Syracuse, where he posted consistent production each season. Clark's speed, explosiveness and physical proﬁle are more good than great, but he likes to play with urgency when driving on plays and arriving with pop. Though the hunger to make plays is there, he doesn't put himself in position to get his hands on the football often enough. Overall, Clark has the versatile skill set and toughness to compete for a nickel role at the next level, but his college tape leaves you wanting more from a playmaking standpoint. His upside on special teams will help his chances of sticking in the NFL.

name: Mike Smith Jr.
summary: Michael "Mike" Smith Jr., one of three kids, grew up in Jacksonville, Fla., with his parents (Lytama and Michael Sr.). He prepped at First Coast High and played across the secondary, notching two interceptions as a senior captain. A three-star recruit, he originally committed to UCF before his senior year before ﬂipping to Appalachian State on signing day. However, he didn't get a chance to play for the coaching staff (led by Eli Drinkwitz) that had recruited him, and he transferred after two years to FCS Eastern Kentucky, where he had an All-America senior season. Smith lined up mostly to the ﬁeld side while also seeing snaps in the box and as a big nickel. With his coverage awareness, he works through route combinations and zeroes in on the eyes of the quarterback to jump throws. He plays with straight-line burst, although he is a tad tightly wound, which hurts his ability for quick recoveries. Smith runs the alley with conviction and paces himself to be a consistent tackle ﬁnisher. Overall, Smith has the athletic proﬁle and ﬁeld awareness to provide depth at multiple safety roles while also making noise on special teams.

name: Keondre Jackson
summary: Keondre Jackson, one of 14 children, was born and raised in Freeport, Ill. He started at receiver and safety for two years at Freeport High, plus qualiﬁed for state in wrestling. A no-star recruit, Jackson signed with Nebraska-Kearney but entered the portal in his ﬁrst semester and transferred to Illinois State, which is closer to home. A three-year starter, his production improved each season, and he generated some buzz after his performance during Senior Bowl week. Jackson is a heavy downhill striker, and his energy pops on tape (defense and special teams). He runs the alley with conviction, using loose feet to make abrupt changes to adjust with shifty ball carriers. His coverage reads and angles tend to be inconsistent from the post, although he keys quickly in underneath zone coverage. Overall, Jackson's average burst and speed aren't ideal, but he is physically imposing as a tackler and projects best near the line of scrimmage where he can man cover tight ends.

name: Zion Childress
summary: Zion Childress, one of three children, was born and raised in Houston with his parents (Cynthia and Deric). Originally a wide receiver at New Caney High, he moved to quarterback and combined for 3,505 passing yards, 2,901 rushing yards and 68 touchdowns over his junior and senior seasons. A three-star recruit, he signed with Texas State as a defensive back and played for two seasons as a nickel. Looking to play at a higher level, he entered the transfer portal and committed to Kentucky (over TCU and Washington). He was a two-time captain for the Wildcats and started 25 straight games as a nickel safety. Although he is undersized, Childress is quick to read and drive to inﬂuence the play. He made a number of plays on the 2024 Georgia tape early in the season but struggled to build off that performance the rest of his ﬁnal year. Overall, Childress is easy to appreciate because he plays fast, physical and decisive, but his missed tackles and lackluster ball production make it tough to fully buy in. His special teams mentality certainly will help.

name: Dean Clark
summary: Dean Clark, the oldest of ﬁve kids, was born and raised in Massillon, Ohio, with his parents (Melissa Battle and William Clark). A safety and wide receiver at Massillon Washington High, he led the team to a 14-1 record and the 2018 Division II state title game as a senior (Clark also advanced to state in track). A three-star recruit, he signed with Kent State and had a breakout 2021 season with a team-best 116 tackles. After an Achilles injury in 2022, he transferred to Fresno State for his ﬁnal two seasons and started 24 combined games. Clark aligned all over the defense, from the box to single high. He reads the backﬁeld action well to anticipate and react and will lay traps for quarterbacks in coverage. His decisiveness as a player really stands out, as it allows him to explode and ﬁnish. His alley angles are generally sharp, and he chases with pace so as to not overrun the ball carrier. fOverall, Clark is a rangy, physical defender with an interchangeable skill set who can provide depth at multiple spots and shine on special teams (680 career special teams snaps in college).

name: Jack Henderson
summary: Jack Henderson grew up outside of New Orleans with his parents (Paige and Steve). An all-around athlete at Mandeville High, he was one of the top lacrosse players in the area and earned all-district honors as a running back and defensive back. A no-star recruit, he received an offer from SE Louisiana and ﬂourished as a three-year starter. He entered the portal after the 2022 season and committed to Minnesota over Louisiana Tech and Louisiana Monroe. Henderson started for two seasons as a hybrid nickel while establishing himself as a core special-teamer. Despite sporting a slender frame, Henderson plays with a contact-driven mentality, but he must be more consistent with his ﬁnishing technique as a tackler. He shows some tightness when making sudden transitions but feels routes coming and ﬂashes ball instincts when he has opportunities. THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 508 Overall, Henderson is a competitive and energetic athlete who has proven himself in a variety of roles and alignments, but special teams could be his ticket to an NFL roster spot.

name: J.J. Roberts
summary: Josiah "J.J." Roberts, one of ﬁve children, grew up near Huntington, W. Va., with his parents (B.J. and Tosha). Two of his younger brothers (Nemo and Zaky) currently play college football at Division II Fairmont State. Roberts was Gatorade Player of the Year in West Virginia as a senior at Cabell Midland High, playing quarterback (in an option offense) and defensive back. A three-star recruit, Roberts was the fourth-ranked player in West Virginia (two spots behind 2024 Steelers second-round pick Zach Frazier), but he was overlooked by the Mountaineers and signed with Wake Forest. After three years, he transferred closer to home and joined Marshall for his ﬁnal two seasons. Roberts has the body type of a cornerback but the mentality of a safety with the way he runs the alley with speed and conviction (led the team in solo tackles in 2024). He explodes into ball carriers, although he often opts for the big hit instead of relying on tackling fundamentals. He plays with impressive range in coverage (led the Sun Belt in passes defended in 2024), although the speed he faced against Ohio State gave him some trouble. Overall, Roberts has the athletic proﬁle, production and playing temperament that could make him a draft pick.

name: Shamari Simmons
summary: Shamari (shuh-MAR-ee) Simmons grew up in Alabama with his parents (Madelin Durrell and Stanford Simmons). His father was a defensive back at Auburn (1999-2001). Shamari Simmons was an all-state athlete in basketball and football at Central High, leading the football team to the 2018 Class 5A state championship as a safety and wide receiver. He started out at Hutchinson (Kan.) Community College before two THE BEAST | BACK TO TABLE OF CONTENTS 509 productive seasons at Austin Peay, then two more at Arizona State. While playing a hybrid nickel role, Simmons did some of his best work near the line of scrimmage, using his burst and physicality to be a disruptive run defender (his run blitz forced a safety in Arizona State's playoff game versus Texas). His motor runs hot, and he explodes with force through the ball carrier as a tackler (has a knack for knocking the ball free). Overall, Simmons brings it every day as a competitor, plays bigger than he looks and has adequate range and ball skills in coverage.

name: Kenyatta Watson II
summary: Kenyatta (ken-YAH-tuh) Watson II grew up in an athletic family. His mother (Janelle) played basketball at Boston College, and his father (Kenyatta Watson Sr.) played wide receiver at Boston College before becoming a high school coach and later a college personnel staffer (currently director of recruiting research and strategy at Auburn). Kenyatta Watson II was an All-American cornerback at Grayson High in Loganville, Ga., posting 91 tackles and two interceptions as a senior. A four-star recruit, he signed with Texas but left the team midway through his second season to look for more playing time. He landed at Georgia Tech, where he was a reserve for three seasons. He transferred to Georgia State for his ﬁnal season and led the team with three interceptions, including one versus Georgia Tech in the 2024 opener. Watson is a lean-framed athlete with linear twitch and speed but limited hip ﬂexibility in his transitions. He is more reactive than proactive reading routes and needs to be more consistent ﬁnishing as a tackler. Overall, Watson doesn't have a robust body of work with just one inconsistent season's worth of starting experience, but he has the testing athleticism to get NFL eyes on him.

name: Fernando Mendoza
strengths: ● Tall, good-sized athlete, with adequate build and body strength ● Quickly lines himself up to targets with snappy load and release ● Throws with high-level anticipation and ball placement ● Smart pre-snap; understands where to attack vulnerable matchups ● Good timing and velocity on quick outs, intermediate outs and seam balls 3 Back to table of contents ● Enough juice in his arm to rip every throw he wants (see hole-shot throw on 2025 Iowa tape) ● Stands tough in face of impending contact and gets off throws ● Steady heartbeat, regardless of score or situation, and mistakes don’t linger on his mind ● Not very graceful in creation mode, but it works — can avoid sacks and extend plays with his legs ● Accelerates quickly on QB-lead draw or scrambles and finishes with toughness (see touchdown run in national title game) ● Egoless personality; plays with a genuine love for his teammates ● Always most-prepared player and refuses to be outworked (it makes sense that his football idol is Tom Brady) ● Highly productive in 2025 — put together one of the best QB seasons in Big Ten history
weaknesses: ● Benefited from RPO-heavy offense at Indiana, with a high percentage of first-read throws ● Rarely required to get to third or fourth read, or backside routes ● Guilty of leaving clean pockets and doesn’t like to be stagnant very long ● Deep ball is good but leaves some short and leads others ● Doesn’t always identify unblocked pressures — and pays the price ● Mobility is an asset, but more of a linear athlete and not elusive in tight quarters
summary: A one-year starter at Indiana (and three-year starter overall), Mendoza thrived in offensive coordinator Mike Shanahan’s RPO-heavy offense (every run is tied to a read). He earned starter-level grades from NFL scouts after the 2024 season, despite having three different offensive coordinators in his three seasons at Cal. However, he elevated his profile even further with a special, Heisman-winning performance in 2025 and separated himself as the NFL Draft’s clear QB1. He led the Hoosiers to a perfect 16-0 record and the national championship, capping off the greatest season in school history. Mendoza has an outstanding feel for touch, placement and layering throws, and he’s an elite back-shoulder thrower. He benefited at Indiana from a quick-read offense (non-stop hitches, slants and outs), but he decisively and accurately rips his initial looks. His physical traits are good, not great, but he makes up for that with advanced mental skills. Though not a dynamic athlete, he does just enough to escape pursuit and keep plays alive. With his toughness (both mental and physical), he moves on from negative plays immediately and shows a knack for finding clutch completions in adverse situations. Overall, Mendoza will need to prove himself with more full-field reads in the NFL, but his intuition, throwing accuracy and play confidence are superpowers and will smooth his transition to the next level. He projects as a mid-level NFL starter and a more mobile version of Bernie Kosar.

summary: A one-year starter at Alabama, Simpson operated in the modern-day spread scheme of offensive coordinator Ryan Grubb (Simpson’s third offensive coordinator in four years in Tuscaloosa). He bided his time as an underclassman behind Bryce Young and Jalen Milroe, and he’d earned his degree before throwing his first collegiate touchdown (1,365 days passed between his final high school TD and his first in college). He accounted for 30 touchdowns in 2025 and led the Tide to the SEC championship, although the first half of the season (20 big-time throws, five turnover-worthy plays) was much more consistent than the second (10 and 12, respectively). With his background as the son of a longtime college coach, Simpson received a quarterback education from a young age, and it shows in his mechanics and operation. He doesn’t have any top-tier physical traits but displays a good-enough arm and the mobility to move the launch point (left or right) on naked keepers/boots. He is generally an accurate passer who can digest defensive concepts and read out the entire field. However, he made just 15 career starts, and that lack of experience manifests in his decision-making and precision. He eliminates things quickly — but often too quickly and turns down throws about to come open. Overall, Simpson has the command and process of an NFL quarterback, but he needs valuable experience to be more efficient in his reads, and to better understand what is open and what isn’t. He projects as a low-level NFL starter, with the ceiling of a mid-level starter and floor of a backup (reminiscent of Daniel Jones with lesser physical traits).

summary: A two-year starter at LSU, Nussmeier operated in former offensive coordinator Joe Sloan’s balanced, RPO-based offense. After backing up Jayden Daniels for two seasons, he earned his own first-round buzz from NFL scouts with a productive 2024 season. However, his senior year was a disappointment, brought on by a perfect storm of contributing factors, including an inconsistent offensive line and a run game that ranked 124th in the FBS. Nussmeier wasn’t blameless for the Tigers’ offensive struggles, although the root of his issues was a preseason abdominal injury, which restricted his movements and prematurely ended his 2025 season. Nussmeier is an undersized, strong-armed passer who can efficiently deliver from various arm slots without sacrificing velocity. He can make any throw he wants and isn’t shy about testing quick-expiring windows, although those overconfident decisions lead to turnovers. As the son of a longtime college and NFL coach, it isn’t a surprise that he shows anticipation when reading out the field, toughness to negotiate muddy pockets and the intangibles that should translate to an NFL quarterback room. Overall, Nussmeier is an aggressive competitor who can throw you into or out of games, but his arm talent and command are foundational traits that generally translate well to the NFL. He projects as a high-level backup and spot starter.

summary: A three-year starter at Penn State, Allar operated both under center and out of the shotgun in former offensive coordinator Andy Kotelnicki’s RPO-based, balanced offense. He opened his collegiate career with an FBS-record 311 passing attempts without an interception and showed progress over his first three years on campus. He finished with 73 total touchdowns (third most in school history), but his senior season was marred with inconsistency before he suffered a season-ending ankle injury, which also sidelined him for most of the draft process. With rare size for a QB, Allar can drive the ball with ease and generally makes sound decisions, although issues pop up when he is late to pull the trigger. He tends to get overly conservative with his reads, which leads to second-guessing, and needs more reps to continue developing his passing instincts (didn’t start playing quarterback until high school). He is better than expected as a scrambler (81 first downs as a ball carrier over 35 career starts). Overall, Allar is a sturdy, strong-armed passer with promising intangibles, 9 Back to table of contents but underdeveloped timing disrupts his ability to execute at a high level. He has NFL starting-caliber physical tools, although a lack of natural passing rhythm creates uncertainty about his developmental ceiling.

summary: A one-year starter at North Dakota State, Payton was a multi-faceted weapon in offensive coordinator Dan Larson’s run-first offense. He turned down FBS options out of high school and hoped to see early playing time for the Bison, who were losing Trey Lance to the NFL. But Cam Miller won the starting job, so Payton served as his backup for four seasons. After accounting for 23 total touchdowns as a reserve in mop-up duty or special packages, he became the starter in 2025 and set school records for total offense per game (268.9) and per play (9.71). Going into the 2025 season, NFL teams saw Payton as an intriguing potential tight end convert, because of his size, athleticism and toughness. But that changed throughout the 2025 season. As a passer, he has a strong left arm, with the stature and aggressive mindset to attack every level of the field. His mechanics, release and accuracy are highly varied, and he doesn’t always trust his anticipation, which reflects his lack of experience. However, his mobility and run strength are separating factors (29 carries of 10-plus yards in 2025). Overall, Payton is green and will require patience, but he’s a dynamic dual-threat quarterback. His physical tools and competitive makeup are promising qualities for a developmental prospect.

And I think he earned that.") ● Georgia’s holder on field goal and PAT attempts ● Played in a lot of big games — finished 37-6 as a starter (24-3 at Georgia; 13-3 at Miami)

summary: A one-year starter at Miami (and three-year starter overall), Beck was productive in offensive coordinator Shannon Dawson’s balanced scheme. After winning two national titles as a backup to Stetson Bennett at Georgia, he stacked promising starts in 2023 before an up-and-down 2024 (without Brock Bowers and Ladd McConkey), which ended unceremoniously with elbow surgery. Beck received a hefty paycheck to transfer to the Hurricanes, and he helped Miami reach the 2025 national championship game — although, his final play at both Georgia and Miami was a turnover. A technically sound passer with a fluid release, Beck processes well, both pre- and post-snap, and spins an accurate ball when his eyes/mechanics stay on time and connected. However, his poise breaks down versus pressure, which leads to forced throws and turnovers (he accounted for a combined 14 turnovers in his six career losses). Though he has some mobility to buy time, he will have a tough time creating off script when facing NFL speed. Overall, Beck is a cerebral pocket passer who can lead drives when the offense stays in rhythm, but he isn’t a proven second-reaction quarterback when things don’t go according to plan. He projects as an NFL backup and potential spot starter.

summary: A two-year starter at Arkansas (and four-year starter overall), Green was a dual-threat quarterback in former offensive coordinator Bobby Petrino’s balanced, spread scheme. After three years at Boise State, he blossomed in Fayetteville and in 2025 ranked No. 3 in the SEC in total yards per game (290.9). He has been one of the most productive quarterbacks in college football — over the past two seasons, he ranked No. 1 in the FBS in plays of 10-plus yards (315) and 20-plus yards (109). One of the most physically gifted players in the 2026 draft class (at any position), Green is big, athletic and competes with NFL-required toughness. He is a playmaker outside the pocket (with both his arm and legs), and his highlight package is full of “wow” moments. However, he is inconsistent working through his reads, and you hold your breath every time he throws over the middle. He takes too many unnecessary chances — he committed a combined 37 turnovers the past two seasons (20 interceptions, 17 fumbles). Overall, Green needs to take better care of the football and refine his mechanics and passing rhythm, but he offers the physical traits and high character worth molding in a read-option, vertical passing game. 14 Back to table of contents

summary: A three-year starter at Clemson, Klubnik was efficient in former offensive coordinator Garrett Riley’s balanced, RPO-based scheme (primarily “11” personnel). The top-ranked quarterback recruit four years ago, he started 40 games for the Tigers and finished No. 3 in school history in career passing yards, behind only Tajh Boyd and Deshaun Watson. However, he was inconsistent as a senior and struggled to build off a productive junior year. Klubnik delivers with above-average touch to all levels of the field and shows enough arm strength to drive the ball down the seam or outside the numbers, when his mechanics are sound. He is light on his feet and comfortable moving the pocket, although he has moments of panic under duress, which lead to bad habits and rushed decisions. Overall, Klubnik is a smooth-twitch athlete with the arm talent to make big-time throws, but his inconsistent pocket presence and urgency reading the field need to be addressed. Projecting as a backup, he would benefit from a rollout, rhythm-based passing game to help open throwing lanes.
